sections.title: Rebuke, confession, and surrender
sections.lead: Kṛṣṇa's first response is a stinging rebuke; Arjuna answers with the strongest form of his dilemma, then admits his confusion and asks to be taught.
reconstruction: Kṛṣṇa first tries the language of honor. Arjuna's despair is unworthy of a noble warrior and will bring disgrace, so he should stand up. Arjuna answers that the issue is not courage. How can one shoot arrows at those one should worship? Better to beg than to enjoy blood-smeared pleasures. Neither outcome of the war is good. Then something changes. Arjuna stops arguing and admits that his own nature is damaged and his mind confused about dharma. He no longer claims to know what is right. He asks to be taught. Having said "I will not fight," he falls silent. Kṛṣṇa, smiling, begins to speak.
insight: The section dramatizes a precondition of learning: the collapse of one's own certainty. While Arjuna argued in Chapter 1, he was still confident in his reasoning. Only when he confesses that his reasoning itself is clouded does teaching become possible. Philosophically, this is the recognition that the faculty that judges, the *buddhi*, can itself be distorted, which is exactly what Kṛṣṇa will address with the "yoga of understanding." Kṛṣṇa's failed first move matters too. Shame does not work on someone with a real moral objection. The Gītā shows its teacher adjusting his method to the student, a pattern it will repeat many times.
sources: The ideal of the disciple who approaches a teacher in humility echoes the Upaniṣads (e.g., *Muṇḍaka* 1.2.12: approach a teacher "fuel in hand"). The structure of crisis followed by request for instruction also opens the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad*, where Naciketas, granted three boons by Death, asks about what lies beyond death.
context: Many philosophical traditions begin with an admission of ignorance: Socratic *aporia*, Augustine's restlessness in the *Confessions*, Descartes's resolve to doubt. The Gītā's version is distinctive in being personal and urgent. Arjuna must act within hours.
matters: Admitting that one's own judgment may be compromised is the hardest and most important step in any serious inquiry, moral, therapeutic or intellectual.
questions: Why does Kṛṣṇa's appeal to honor fail? What does that teach about moral persuasion?
What exactly does Arjuna confess in 2.7? Is the confession itself a moral achievement?
How do you read Kṛṣṇa's smile in 2.10?

premises.label: Arjuna's grief is unworthy of a warrior
premises.text: Kṛṣṇa's first, failed appeal to honor.

premises.label: Neither victory nor defeat would be good
premises.text: Arjuna restates the dilemma at its strongest.

claim.label: Arjuna surrenders his certainty and asks to be taught
claim.text: The pivot of the Gītā: confession of confusion and request for instruction.

implications.label: Teaching can now begin
implications.text: Kṛṣṇa, smiling, starts the real instruction.

sections.title: The undying self
sections.lead: Kṛṣṇa's first argument: the self is eternal and cannot be killed; grief rests on mistaking what we are.
reconstruction: Kṛṣṇa's first argument is that Arjuna's grief rests on a mistake about what a person is. What is real does not cease to be, and what is unreal does not come to be {2.16}. The body is unreal in this sense: it comes and goes. The embodied self is real. It passed through childhood, youth and age without perishing {2.13} and passes through death the same way {2.22}. Weapons, fire and water cannot touch it {2.23}. So no one is really killed in battle {2.19}. Grief over the dead or the living is misplaced {2.11}. The argument closes with a fallback {2.26–27}. Even if the self were born and died constantly, death would be certain for whatever is born. Grieving over the inevitable is therefore pointless on any view.
insight: The argument is powerful but strange. Its strength is that it attacks the root of Arjuna's distress: the identification of persons with their bodies. Its strangeness is that, taken alone, it seems to prove too much. If no one is ever killed, then killing is morally neutral, and so is saving life. Critics from early Western Indologists to contemporary ethicists have pointed out that such an argument could justify any violence. The tradition's best reply is that the argument is not a justification of killing but a cure for one particular delusion: the grief-paralysis that makes a person unable to act at all. It must be read together with what follows. The self's eternity removes *fear and grief*. It does not settle *what ought to be done*. That is the work of dharma (2.31–38) and of the yoga of understanding (2.39ff.). The fallback argument of 2.26–27 also shows Kṛṣṇa's pedagogy. He does not stake everything on one metaphysics.
sources: Close parallels with the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad* (2.7, 2.18–19) are certain. The self as unborn, eternal and indestructible is the core of Upaniṣadic teaching (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka* 4.4.22–25: "this self is not this, not this… it does not tremble, it is not harmed"). The axiom of 2.16 also resembles the *Chāndogya*'s argument (6.2.1–2) that being cannot come from non-being.
context: The section invites comparison with Plato's *Phaedo*, where Socrates, facing death, argues for the soul's immortality and chides his friends for weeping. Both use metaphysics to transform grief. It also invites comparison with Buddhism's denial of a permanent self (*anātman*). The Gītā's 2.26 seems to address that view directly. Modern philosophy of personal identity (Locke, Parfit) asks what persists through change, the very question of 2.13.
matters: How we understand ourselves shapes how we grieve, fear and act. Whatever one thinks of the metaphysics, the section asks a question every person faces: what am I, if I am not my body's fate?
questions: Does the argument from the self's immortality prove too much? How would Kṛṣṇa answer that objection?
Compare the clothing image (2.22) with Socrates in the *Phaedo*. Is either consoling? To whom?
What work does the fallback argument of 2.26–27 do? Why include it?
Read 2.16 slowly. What does it mean for something to be "real" in this sense?

premises.label: The real never ceases to be
premises.text: Being and non-being cannot turn into each other.

premises.label: The self passes through changes without perishing
premises.text: Childhood, youth, age, and death are changes of body, not of self.

premises.label: The self cannot be harmed
premises.text: It neither kills nor is killed; weapons and fire do not touch it.

claim.label: Grief for the dead and living is misplaced
claim.text: Arjuna's sorrow rests on a mistake about what persons are.

implications.label: Even on other views, grief over the inevitable is pointless
implications.text: A fallback argument that works without the metaphysics.

implications.label: The self's eternity cures fear, but does not yet say what to do
implications.text: That question is answered by dharma and by the yoga of understanding.

sections.title: The warrior's own dharma
sections.lead: Kṛṣṇa's second argument appeals to Arjuna's own duty as a warrior, to honor and to heaven, and ends with the first statement of equanimity.
reconstruction: Kṛṣṇa now argues on the level Arjuna himself had appealed to: dharma. Arjuna's dharma is that of a warrior, and for a warrior nothing is better than a just war {2.31}. To abandon it would be to abandon both duty and honor and to incur evil {2.33}. People would say he fled from fear {2.35}. Either outcome, death or victory, is good for him {2.37}. Then comes the decisive qualification. He should fight treating victory and defeat alike {2.38}, and only so will he avoid evil.
insight: The section is a rhetorical bridge. It meets Arjuna where he is, in a world of dharma, honor and heaven, and then, in its final verse, quietly prepares to leave that world behind. The appeal to disgrace is a "lower" motive, and Kṛṣṇa knows it. The equanimity of 2.38 is not about honor at all. Many commentators read this structure as Kṛṣṇa's skillful means: lower motives are invoked only to be transcended. There is a real tension here. Arjuna had argued from *family* dharma (1.40). Kṛṣṇa argues from *class* dharma. Neither is the final word. The Gītā will finally speak of a dharma that is God's to protect (4.7) and then of abandoning all dharmas (18.66). Readers should notice how many layers of "duty" the text contains.
sources: The warrior's duty to fight and the promise of heaven for those slain facing the enemy are standard in the Dharmaśāstras (e.g., *Manu* 7.87–89). The epic's warrior ethos (*kṣatra-dharma*) is debated within the Mahābhārata itself, notably by Yudhiṣṭhira, who repeatedly questions it.
context: The appeal to role-duty and honor recalls Homer's Sarpedon (*Iliad* 12): the nobles must fight in front because they are honored. Contemporary role-ethics (and debates about professional duty: the lawyer, the soldier) asks how far a role can justify acts that private morality would forbid.
matters: Most people meet the question "should I?" through roles: parent, employee, citizen, soldier. The section asks how far a role's duties bind us, and hints that they bind best when performed without craving for reward or fear of shame.
questions: Is Kṛṣṇa's appeal to honor and heaven sincere, or merely tactical? What is the evidence in the text?
How does 2.38 change the meaning of the preceding verses?
Arjuna appealed to family dharma, Kṛṣṇa to warrior dharma. How should conflicts between dharmas be resolved?

premises.label: A just war is a warrior's highest duty
premises.text: For a kṣatriya, nothing is better than a dharmic battle.

premises.label: Refusing would bring disgrace and evil
premises.text: Abandoning duty and honor is itself a wrong.

claim.label: Fight, as your dharma requires
claim.text: Either outcome is good; so stand up and fight.

implications.label: But fight with equanimity
implications.text: Treat victory and defeat alike. Only then is the act free of evil. This opens the next teaching.

sections.title: The yoga of understanding: action without attachment
sections.lead: Kṛṣṇa announces a new teaching: act with a resolute, single understanding, renounce the fruits, and let equanimity be your yoga.
reconstruction: Kṛṣṇa now shifts the ground. What matters is not only *that* one acts but the *understanding* (*buddhi*) from which one acts. An understanding that is resolute is single. One scattered among desires is many-branched {2.41}. The ritualists who use the Veda to get heaven and power have scattered minds {2.42–44}. One should go beyond the guṇas, beyond the pairs of opposites, beyond acquiring and keeping {2.45}. The practical rule follows. One has a right to the action, never to its fruit. Do not act for the fruit, and do not fall into inaction {2.47}. Act steadily, giving up attachment, the same in success and failure {2.48}. Such action does not bind. It leaves behind both good and bad deeds {2.50}. When the understanding passes beyond delusion and stands firm in concentration, one reaches yoga {2.52–53}.
insight: This is the conceptual heart of karma-yoga and arguably of the Gītā. Its decisive move is to separate two things ordinarily fused: *doing* something and *staking oneself on its outcome*. The agent is responsible for the act, its rightness and skill, but not owner of the results. This dissolves the renunciant's dilemma. Action binds through attachment, and one can act without attachment. Critics have raised two objections. First, can one act intentionally without caring about results? Intentional action seems to *aim* at outcomes. The best reply is that 2.47 forbids making the fruit one's *motive* (*hetu*), not foreseeing it. The agent aims at doing the right act well, and the outcome follows or does not. Second, does indifference to consequences license recklessness? Here 18.25 helps: action "without regard to consequences" is called tamasic. The Gītā wants attention to consequences without anxiety about them. That distinction is fine but real.
sources: The critique of desire-driven ritual draws on Upaniṣadic criticism of sacrifice (*Muṇḍaka* 1.2.7–10 calls ritualists "fools" who return again to this world). The single-pointed understanding resembles the *Kaṭha*'s image of the disciplined intellect as charioteer (*Kaṭha* 3.3–9). The *Īśā Upaniṣad* 2 ("action does not cling to a person") is the nearest anticipation of 2.47.
context: Comparisons abound. Kant's good will, whose worth lies not in what it accomplishes but in its principle, is a near cousin. So is Stoic ethics (Epictetus, *Enchiridion* 1): some things are up to us (our acts and judgments), others not (outcomes), and freedom lies in caring only for the former. Both T. S. Eliot ("And do not think of the fruit of action. / Fare forward," *Four Quartets*) and Gandhi took 2.47 as a life-rule. Modern psychology's distinction between "process" and "outcome" goals, and research on performance anxiety, give the verse an empirical dimension.
matters: Most suffering in work and relationships comes not from effort but from anxious attachment to results we cannot control. These verses offer a way to act wholeheartedly while staying free, a teaching that has helped soldiers, athletes, activists and ordinary workers.
questions: Can a person act intentionally without making the outcome their motive? Construct an example.
What is the difference between not caring about consequences and not being attached to them?
Compare 2.47 with Epictetus's distinction between what is and is not "up to us." Where do they differ?
Why does Kṛṣṇa add "do not be attached to inaction"? What misreading does it prevent?

premises.label: Action binds through attachment to its fruit
premises.text: Not action itself but the ego's stake in outcomes creates bondage.

premises.label: A resolute understanding is single, not scattered
premises.text: Desire-driven minds are many-branched.

claim.label: Act without attachment, the same in success and failure
claim.text: Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits. Equanimity is yoga.

implications.label: Such action does not bind
implications.text: One leaves behind good and bad deeds and reaches the place beyond sorrow.

implications.label: Ritual for rewards is superseded
implications.text: The Veda's purposes are fulfilled in the knower's understanding.

sections.title: The person of steady wisdom
sections.lead: Arjuna asks what the sage is like; Kṛṣṇa answers with a portrait of equanimity, sense-mastery and peace.
reconstruction: Kṛṣṇa's answer is a description, not a rule. The sage is content in the self, so desires lose their grip {2.55}. The sage is unshaken in sorrow and without craving in pleasure {2.56}, withdraws the senses at will {2.58}, and controls them by turning toward the highest {2.61}. The reason control matters is given in a precise psychology: brooding on objects breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, frustrated desire becomes anger, anger clouds memory and understanding, and the person is destroyed {2.62–63}. By contrast, one who moves among objects without attraction or aversion gains serenity, and in serenity sorrow ends {2.64–65}. Such a person is like the ocean, full and still while rivers pour in {2.70}. Without "mine" and without I-making, he reaches the peace of brahman {2.71–72}.
insight: The passage is a phenomenology of freedom. Its insight is that the problem is not the senses or the world but *dwelling* (*dhyāyataḥ*) on objects, the mind's repeated return to what it wants. The chain of 2.62–63 is a remarkably modern model, in which attention drives appetite, appetite drives frustration, and frustration distorts cognition. The portrait also resolves an apparent paradox: how can one act fully without desire? The sage is not without inclinations (the "rivers" keep coming) but is not *moved* by them. The ideal is not a stone but an ocean, full and therefore undisturbed. One tension remains. The sage here "withdraws" and is "free of longing," while Arjuna is asked to fight. The portrait describes the inner state from which action should come, not a withdrawal from action. That reconciliation is the work of Chapter 3.
sources: The tortoise image and the restraint of the senses appear in the epic's *Mokṣadharma* and in *Manu* 7.105. The chariot model of *Kaṭha* 3.3–9 lies behind the passage on the senses carrying off the mind (2.60, 2.67). The ocean image recalls *Muṇḍaka* 3.2.8 (rivers merging in the sea).
context: Stoic *apatheia* and the Epicurean *ataraxia* (tranquility) are close parallels, as is the Buddhist account of craving (*taṇhā*) arising from contact and feeling in the twelvefold chain of dependent origination. Contemporary cognitive science of craving, and mindfulness-based interventions for addiction, explicitly describe the "elaboration" of desire through rumination, the *dhyāyataḥ* of 2.62. Gandhi had 2.54–72 recited every evening at his prayer meetings.
matters: The passage offers a picture of a free and peaceful person who is not cut off from the world, and a precise account of how we lose that freedom. It is one of the most practically useful pages in world literature.
questions: Trace the chain of 2.62–63 in an experience of your own. Where could it be broken?
What is the difference between suppressing a desire and losing the taste for it (2.59)?
Is the ocean (2.70) a better image of the ideal than the tortoise (2.58)? What does each emphasize?
Why might Gandhi, an activist, have chosen these verses for daily recitation?

premises.label: Dwelling on objects breeds desire, anger and ruin
premises.text: A causal chain from attention to destruction.

premises.label: Moving among objects without attraction or aversion brings serenity
premises.text: Control of the senses yields clarity and the end of sorrow.

claim.label: The sage is content in the self and unshaken
claim.text: Full like the ocean, the sage is not moved by desires that still arise.

implications.label: Without "mine" and I-making, one reaches peace
implications.text: Freedom from possessiveness is the key to peace.

implications.label: The state of brahman, even at death
implications.text: The goal of the teaching is named.

chapters.title: The Yoga of Action

verses.text: If you hold that understanding is superior to action, Janārdana, then why do you urge me to this terrible action, Keśava?
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: Your words seem to conflict, and they confuse my understanding. Tell me decisively the one thing by which I may reach the better [*śreyas*].
In this world, sinless one, I taught long ago a twofold foundation: the yoga of knowledge [*jñāna-yoga*] for followers of Sāṅkhya, and the yoga of action [*karma-yoga*] for yogins.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: A person does not reach freedom from action [*naiṣkarmya*] by not undertaking actions, nor reach perfection by renunciation [*saṁnyāsa*] alone.
No one can remain even for a moment without acting. The guṇas born of nature [*prakṛti*] make everyone act, whether they will it or not.
One who restrains the organs of action but sits remembering sense objects with the mind is a deluded self, called a hypocrite.
But one who controls the senses with the mind, Arjuna, and without attachment undertakes the yoga of action with the organs of action, excels.
Perform your prescribed [*niyata*] action, for action is better than inaction. Without action you could not even maintain your body.
This world is bound by action, except for action done for the sake of sacrifice [*yajña*]. Perform action for that purpose, son of Kuntī, free from attachment.
Long ago, having created creatures together with sacrifice, the Lord of creatures [*Prajāpati*] said: "By this you shall multiply. Let this be your wish-fulfilling cow.
Nourish the gods with this, and let the gods nourish you. Nourishing one another, you will reach the highest good.
Nourished by sacrifice, the gods will give you the enjoyments you desire." One who enjoys their gifts without giving to them in return is simply a thief.
The good, who eat what remains from the sacrifice, are released from all faults. The wicked, who cook only for themselves, eat evil.
Beings arise from food; food arises from rain; rain arises from sacrifice; sacrifice arises from action.
Know that action arises from brahman [here, the Veda], and brahman arises from the imperishable. Therefore the all-pervading brahman is always established in sacrifice.
One who does not keep turning the wheel set in motion here lives an evil life, delighting in the senses. That one lives in vain, Pārtha.
But the person who delights in the self alone, content in the self and satisfied in the self alone, has nothing that must be done.
That person gains nothing by acting here and nothing by not acting, and depends on no being for any purpose.
Therefore, without attachment, always perform the action that must be done. By performing action without attachment, a person reaches the highest.
Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone. You too should act, looking to the holding-together of the world [*loka-saṅgraha*].
Whatever the best person does, others do too. Whatever standard that one sets, the world follows.
For me, Pārtha, there is nothing whatever to be done in the three worlds, and nothing unattained to attain. Yet I continue in action.
For if I ever ceased to act tirelessly, Pārtha, people would follow my path in every way.
If I did not perform action, these worlds would perish. I would cause confusion and destroy these creatures.
The unwise act attached to action, Bhārata. The wise should act in the same way but without attachment, wishing to hold the world together.
The wise should not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant who are attached to action. Acting with yoga themselves, they should lead them to delight in all actions.
Actions are performed in every case by the guṇas of nature, but one deluded by I-making thinks, "I am the doer."
But one who knows the truth about how the guṇas and their actions are divided, mighty-armed one, thinks "guṇas are moving among guṇas" and is not attached.
Those deluded by the guṇas of nature are attached to the actions of the guṇas. One who knows the whole should not unsettle the slow-witted who know only in part.
Surrender all actions to me with your mind on the inner self [*adhyātma*]. Free from longing and from "mine," fight, with your fever gone.
Those who always follow this teaching of mine, full of faith and without grumbling, are also freed from actions.
But those who grumble at it and do not follow my teaching are bewildered in all knowledge. Know them to be lost and mindless.
Even the wise person acts according to his own nature. Beings follow nature. What will restraint accomplish?
Attraction and aversion lie in wait in the objects of each sense. One should not come under their power, for they are one's enemies on the road.
Better one's own dharma, though imperfect, than another's dharma well performed. Better death in one's own dharma; another's dharma is dangerous.
Then what drives a person to commit evil, Vārṣṇeya, even unwillingly, as if forced?
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: It is desire, it is anger, born of the guṇa of rajas: all-devouring and greatly evil. Know it as the enemy here.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: As fire is covered by smoke, a mirror by dust, and an embryo by the womb, so this [knowledge] is covered by that [desire].
Knowledge is covered, son of Kuntī, by this constant enemy of the wise, which takes the form of desire, an insatiable fire.
The senses, the mind, and the understanding are said to be its seat. Through these it covers knowledge and deludes the embodied one.
Therefore, bull of the Bhāratas, first control the senses. Then kill this evil thing, which destroys knowledge and discernment [*jñāna-vijñāna*].
The senses are high, they say. Higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the understanding; but what is higher than the understanding is *he* [the self].
Knowing what is higher than the understanding, steady the self by the self, mighty-armed one, and kill the enemy that takes the form of desire, so hard to overcome.

chapters.title: The Yoga of Knowledge and the Renunciation of Action

verses.text: I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat [the sun]. Vivasvat told it to Manu, and Manu told it to Ikṣvāku.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Handed down in this succession, the royal seers knew it. But with the long passage of time, scorcher of foes, this yoga was lost here.
Today I have declared this same ancient yoga to you, for you are my devotee and my friend. This is the supreme secret.
Your birth was later and Vivasvat's was earlier. How am I to understand that you taught it in the beginning?
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: Many births of mine have passed, Arjuna, and many of yours. I know them all, but you do not know them, scorcher of foes.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Though I am unborn and my self is imperishable, though I am lord of beings, I come into being by my own power [*ātma-māyā*], governing my own nature.
Whenever dharma declines, Bhārata, and adharma rises, then I send myself forth.
To protect the good, to destroy evildoers, and to establish dharma, I come into being age after age [*yuge yuge*].
One who truly knows my divine birth and action is not born again on leaving the body. That one comes to me, Arjuna.
Free from passion, fear, and anger, absorbed in me and taking refuge in me, purified by the austerity of knowledge, many have come to my state of being.
In whatever way people approach me, in that way I share myself with them [*bhajāmi*]. Everywhere, Pārtha, people follow my path.
Wanting success from their actions, people here sacrifice to the gods, for in the human world success born of action comes quickly.
I created the four social orders [*cātur-varṇya*] according to the division of guṇa and action. Though I am their maker, know me as the non-doer, imperishable.
tnotes: The verse grounds the four social orders in *guṇa* and *karma* (quality and action), not explicitly in birth. Readers have long debated whether birth is implied.

verses.text: Actions do not taint me, and I have no longing for their fruit. One who knows me in this way is not bound by actions.
Knowing this, the ancient seekers of liberation also performed action. So perform action, as the ancients did long ago.
What is action? What is inaction? Even the wise are confused here. I will explain action to you, and knowing it you will be freed from evil.
One must understand action, understand wrong action [*vikarma*], and understand inaction. The way of action is deep.
One who sees inaction in action and action in inaction is wise among humans. That one is yoked, even while performing all action.
When all of a person's undertakings are free of desire and intention [*saṅkalpa*], and that person's actions are burned up in the fire of knowledge, the wise call that person learned.
Abandoning attachment to the fruit of action, always content and dependent on nothing, such a person does nothing at all, even while engaged in action.
Without longing, with mind and self restrained, giving up all possessions, doing action with the body alone, one incurs no fault.
Content with whatever comes by chance, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy, the same in success and failure, such a person is not bound even when acting.
When a person's attachment is gone and he is free, with mind established in knowledge and acting for the sake of sacrifice, his action dissolves entirely.
The offering is brahman; the oblation is brahman, poured by brahman into the fire that is brahman. One who sees brahman in action, as in concentration, will reach brahman.
Some yogins offer sacrifice to the gods alone; others offer sacrifice, by sacrifice itself, into the fire of brahman.
Some offer hearing and the other senses into the fires of restraint; others offer sound and the other objects into the fires of the senses.
Others offer all the actions of the senses and of the vital breath into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge.
Others sacrifice with material goods, with austerity, or with yoga, and ascetics of strict vows sacrifice through study and knowledge.
Others, intent on breath-control, offer the in-breath into the out-breath and the out-breath into the in-breath, restraining the course of both.
Others, restricting their food, offer breaths into breaths. All of these know sacrifice, and their faults are destroyed by sacrifice.
Eating the nectar that remains from sacrifice, they go to eternal brahman. This world is not for one who does not sacrifice, best of Kurus, much less the next.
Many kinds of sacrifice are spread out like this in the mouth of brahman. Know that they are all born of action. Knowing this, you will be freed.
Sacrifice made of knowledge is better than sacrifice of material things, scorcher of foes. All action without exception, Pārtha, culminates in knowledge.
Learn this by bowing down, by inquiry, and by service. The wise who see the truth will teach you knowledge.
Knowing it, Pāṇḍava, you will not fall into delusion like this again. By it you will see all beings without exception in the self, and then in me.
Even if you were the worst of all evildoers, the boat of knowledge alone would carry you across all wickedness.
As a kindled fire reduces its fuel to ashes, Arjuna, so the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes.
Nothing here purifies like knowledge. One perfected in yoga finds it, in time, within oneself.
One who has faith [*śraddhā*], is intent on knowledge, and restrains the senses gains it. Having gained knowledge, one soon reaches supreme peace.
The ignorant self, without faith and full of doubt, perishes. For the doubter there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness.
Actions do not bind one who has renounced action through yoga, whose doubt has been cut away by knowledge, and who possesses the self, Dhanañjaya.
So take the sword of knowledge and cut this doubt in your heart, born of ignorance. Resort to yoga. Stand up, Bhārata!

chapters.title: The Yoga of Renunciation

verses.text: You praise renunciation of actions, Kṛṣṇa, and then again yoga. Tell me decisively which of the two is better.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: Renunciation and the yoga of action both lead to the highest good. But of the two, the yoga of action is better than renunciation of action.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Know as a constant renunciant the one who neither hates nor desires. Free of the pairs of opposites, mighty-armed one, one is easily freed from bondage.
Children, not the wise, speak of Sāṅkhya and yoga as different. One truly established in either finds the fruit of both.
The yogins reach the same state that the followers of Sāṅkhya reach. One who sees Sāṅkhya and yoga as one truly sees.
But renunciation, mighty-armed one, is hard to attain without yoga. The sage who is yoked in yoga soon reaches brahman.
One yoked in yoga is pure in self, self-conquered, and master of the senses. When one's self has become the self of all beings, one is not tainted even when acting.
The yoked knower of truth thinks, "I do nothing at all." While seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing,
speaking, releasing, grasping, opening and closing the eyes, such a one holds that only the senses are moving among the objects of the senses.
One who acts while placing all actions in brahman and abandoning attachment is not stained by evil, just as a lotus leaf is not stained by water.
To purify themselves, yogins abandon attachment and perform action with the body, the mind, the understanding, or even the senses alone.
The yoked one, abandoning the fruit of action, attains abiding peace. The unyoked one, attached to the fruit and driven by desire, is bound.
Renouncing all actions with the mind, the embodied one sits happily in control, in the city of nine gates [the body], neither acting nor causing action.
The Lord [*prabhu*] does not create agency or actions for the world, nor the link between action and fruit. It is inherent nature [*svabhāva*] that is at work.
The all-pervading one does not take on anyone's evil or good deed. Knowledge is covered by ignorance, and that is why beings are deluded.
But for those in whom ignorance is destroyed by knowledge of the self, that knowledge lights up the supreme, like the sun.
Their understanding is on that, their self in that, they are established in that and intent on that. Their faults cleansed by knowledge, they go where there is no return.
The wise see the same in a learned and humble brāhmaṇa, in a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste [*śva-pāka*, "one who cooks dogs"].
Even here, those whose minds rest in sameness have overcome the cycle of creation. Brahman is flawless and the same in all, so they are established in brahman.
One should not rejoice on getting what is pleasant nor be shaken on getting what is unpleasant. Steady in understanding and undeluded, the knower of brahman is established in brahman.
With the self unattached to outer contacts, one finds happiness in the self. With the self yoked in the yoga of brahman, one reaches imperishable happiness.
The enjoyments born of contact are wombs of sorrow. They have a beginning and an end, son of Kuntī, and the wise do not delight in them.
One who can withstand, here before leaving the body, the agitation born of desire and anger, is yoked. That one is a happy person.
The yogin whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within becomes brahman and reaches the nirvāṇa of brahman.
Seers whose faults are destroyed and whose doubts are cut away, who are self-controlled and delight in the welfare of all beings, reach the nirvāṇa of brahman.
For ascetics who are free of desire and anger, whose thought is controlled and who know the self, the nirvāṇa of brahman is near on every side.
Shutting out outer contacts, fixing the gaze between the eyebrows, and evening out the in-breath and out-breath that move within the nostrils,
the sage whose senses, mind, and understanding are controlled, who is intent on release, and from whom desire, fear, and anger have departed, is forever free.
Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great lord of all the worlds, the friend of all beings, one reaches peace.

chapters.title: The Yoga of Meditation

verses.text: One who performs the action that should be done, without depending on its fruit, is a renunciant and a yogin. One who merely gives up the sacred fires and the rites is not.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: What they call renunciation, Pāṇḍava, know to be yoga. No one becomes a yogin without renouncing intention [*saṅkalpa*].
For the sage who wishes to climb to yoga, action is said to be the means. Once that same sage has climbed to yoga, calm [*śama*] is said to be the means.
When one is not attached to sense objects or to actions and has renounced all intentions, one is said to have climbed to yoga.
One should lift up the self by the self and not let the self sink down. For the self alone is the self's friend, and the self alone is the self's enemy.
For one who has conquered the self by the self, the self is a friend. But for one who has not conquered the self, the self acts with hostility, like an enemy.
For one who is self-conquered and at peace, the supreme self stays concentrated in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor.
A yogin is called yoked when the self is satisfied with knowledge and discernment, unshakable, and master of the senses, and when a clod, a stone, and gold are all the same to that person.
One who regards with an equal mind well-wishers, friends, enemies, the indifferent, the neutral, the hateful, and relatives, and the good and the wicked alike, excels.
The yogin should constantly concentrate the self, staying in solitude and alone, with thought and self controlled, free of longing and without possessions.
In a clean place, he should set up for himself a firm seat, neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass.
Sitting there, making the mind one-pointed and controlling the activity of thought and senses, he should practice yoga to purify the self.
He should hold body, head, and neck straight and still, steady, gazing at the tip of his nose and not looking around.
With the self at peace, free of fear, firm in the vow of celibacy [*brahmacarya*], controlling the mind, he should sit yoked, with his thought on me and intent on me.
Always concentrating the self in this way, the yogin with controlled mind reaches the peace that culminates in nirvāṇa and abides in me.
But yoga is not for one who eats too much or for one who does not eat at all, Arjuna, nor for one who sleeps too much or stays awake too long.
For one who is moderate in eating and recreation, moderate in effort in action, and moderate in sleep and waking, yoga destroys sorrow.
When thought is well controlled and rests in the self alone, free from longing for any desire, one is said to be yoked.
"Like a lamp in a windless place, which does not flicker": this is the image given for the yogin whose thought is controlled, practicing the yoga of the self.
Thought comes to rest, restrained by the practice of yoga, and seeing the self by the self, one is content in the self.
One knows that infinite happiness which the understanding grasps and which lies beyond the senses. Established there, one does not move from the truth.
Having gained it, one thinks no other gain greater. Established in it, one is not shaken even by heavy sorrow.
Let that be known as yoga: the unyoking from union with sorrow [*duḥkha-saṁyoga-viyoga*]. That yoga should be practiced with resolve and with a mind that does not lose heart.
Abandon entirely all desires born of intention, and with the mind alone hold back the whole group of senses on every side.
Little by little one should come to rest, with the understanding held firm. Having made the mind abide in the self, one should think of nothing at all.
Whenever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off, one should rein it back from there and bring it under the control of the self.
Supreme happiness comes to the yogin whose mind is tranquil, whose passion is stilled, who has become brahman and is free of fault.
Constantly concentrating the self in this way, the yogin, free of fault, easily attains the infinite happiness of contact with brahman.
One whose self is yoked in yoga and who sees the same everywhere sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self.
One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am not lost to that one, and that one is not lost to me.
The yogin who is established in oneness and worships me as dwelling in all beings abides in me, however he lives.
One who sees the same in everything by comparison with oneself [*ātmaupamya*], Arjuna, whether pleasure or pain, is considered the supreme yogin.
tnotes: *ātmaupamya*, "taking oneself as the measure," is the Gītā's version of the golden rule. Others' pleasure and pain are felt as one's own.

verses.text: You have taught this yoga as sameness, Madhusūdana, but because of restlessness I do not see how it can stand firm.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: For the mind is restless, Kṛṣṇa, turbulent, strong, and stubborn. I think it is as hard to restrain as the wind.
No doubt, mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and hard to restrain. But it is held by practice [*abhyāsa*] and dispassion [*vairāgya*], son of Kuntī.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: I agree that yoga is hard to attain for one whose self is uncontrolled. But one whose self is controlled and who strives can attain it by the right means.
Consider one who has faith but is not controlled, whose mind strays from yoga before reaching perfection in yoga. What path does that one take, Kṛṣṇa?
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: Fallen from both, without support, bewildered on the path to brahman, does he not perish like a scattered cloud, mighty-armed one?
Cut away this doubt of mine completely, Kṛṣṇa, for no one but you can cut it away.
Pārtha, there is no destruction for him, either here or hereafter. No one who does good, my friend, comes to a bad end.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: The one fallen from yoga reaches the worlds of the meritorious and dwells there for countless years. Then he is born in the house of the pure and prosperous.
Or he is born into a family of wise yogins, though such a birth is harder to obtain in this world.
There he regains the understanding he reached in his former body, joy of the Kurus, and from there strives again for perfection.
His former practice carries him along even without his willing it. Even one who only wishes to know yoga goes beyond the word-brahman [the Veda].
But the yogin who strives with effort is purified of faults and perfected through many births. Then he reaches the supreme goal.
The yogin is superior to ascetics, superior even to the learned, and superior to those who perform ritual action. Therefore be a yogin, Arjuna.
And of all yogins, I consider most fully yoked the one who is full of faith and worships me with the inner self absorbed in me.

chapters.title: The Yoga of Knowledge and Discernment

verses.text: Hear, Pārtha, how you will know me completely and without doubt, with your mind attached to me, practicing yoga and relying on me.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: I will teach you this knowledge together with discernment [*jñāna-vijñāna*] in full. Once you know it, nothing further remains to be known here.
Among thousands of people, scarcely one strives for perfection. Of those who strive and are perfected, scarcely one knows me in truth.
Earth, water, fire, wind, space, mind, understanding, and I-making: this is my nature [*prakṛti*], divided eightfold.
This is my lower nature. But know my other, higher nature, mighty-armed one: the principle of life [*jīva-bhūta*], by which this world is sustained.
Understand that all beings have these two as their source. I am the origin and the dissolution of the whole world.
There is nothing whatever higher than me, Dhanañjaya. All this is strung on me like pearls on a thread.
I am the taste in water, son of Kuntī, and the light in moon and sun. I am the syllable Om in all the Vedas, the sound in space, the manhood in men.
I am the pure fragrance in the earth and the brilliance in fire. I am the life in all beings and the austerity in ascetics.
Know me, Pārtha, as the eternal seed of all beings. I am the understanding of those who understand and the splendor of the splendid.
I am the strength of the strong, free from desire and passion. In beings, bull of the Bhāratas, I am the desire that does not oppose dharma.
Whatever states of being there are, whether of sattva, rajas, or tamas, know that they come from me alone. But I am not in them; they are in me.
Deluded by these states made of the three guṇas, this whole world does not recognize me, who am beyond them and imperishable.
This divine māyā of mine, made of the guṇas, is hard to cross. Those who take refuge in me alone cross over this māyā.
Evildoers do not take refuge in me: the deluded, the lowest of humans, whose knowledge is carried off by māyā and who have taken on a demonic nature.
Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the one who knows, bull of the Bhāratas.
Of these the one who knows excels: always yoked and devoted to the One alone. I am exceedingly dear to the one who knows, and that one is dear to me.
All of these are noble, but I regard the one who knows as my very self. With self yoked, that one abides in me alone as the highest goal.
At the end of many births, the one who knows takes refuge in me, thinking "Vāsudeva is all." Such a great self is very rare.
Those whose knowledge is carried off by various desires take refuge in other gods. They follow this or that rule, constrained by their own nature.
Whatever form any devotee wishes to worship with faith, I make that very faith unshakable.
Yoked with that faith, they seek to please that form. From it they obtain their desires, though in truth it is I alone who grant them.
But the fruit for those of small understanding is finite. Those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods; my devotees come to me.
The unintelligent think that I, the unmanifest, have become manifest. They do not know my higher being, imperishable and supreme.
I am not manifest to all, veiled as I am by my yoga-māyā. This deluded world does not recognize me, the unborn and imperishable.
I know the beings that have passed, those that are present, and those yet to come, Arjuna. But no one knows me.
All beings, scorcher of foes, fall into bewilderment at birth, through the delusion of the pairs of opposites, which arises from desire and aversion.
But people of good deeds whose evil has come to an end are freed from the delusion of the pairs, and they worship me with firm vows.
Those who take refuge in me and strive for release from old age and death know that brahman fully. They know the inner self [*adhyātma*] and action in its entirety.
Those who know me together with what pertains to beings [*adhibhūta*], to the gods [*adhidaiva*], and to sacrifice [*adhiyajña*], with minds yoked, know me even at the time of death.

chapters.title: The Yoga of the Imperishable Brahman

verses.text: What is that brahman? What is the inner self? What is action, Supreme Person? What is it that pertains to beings, and what is said to pertain to the gods?
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: What pertains to sacrifice, and how is it here in this body, Madhusūdana? And how are you to be known at the time of death by those who are self-controlled?
Brahman is the supreme imperishable [*akṣara*]. Its own nature [*svabhāva*] is called the inner self. The creative outpouring that brings beings into existence is called action.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: What pertains to beings is perishable existence. What pertains to the gods is the Person [*puruṣa*]. What pertains to sacrifice is I myself, here in the body, best of the embodied.
Whoever leaves the body at the time of death remembering me alone comes to my state of being. Of this there is no doubt.
Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end, to that state one goes, son of Kuntī, having always been shaped by it.
Therefore remember me at all times, and fight. With mind and understanding fixed on me, you will come to me without doubt.
With thought yoked by the yoga of practice, not straying elsewhere, meditating on the supreme divine Person, Pārtha, one goes to him.
He is the seer, the ancient, the ruler, smaller than the minute, the upholder of all, of unthinkable form, sun-colored, beyond darkness.

At the time of departure, one who meditates on him with unmoving mind, yoked with devotion and the power of yoga, and directs the breath fully between the eyebrows, reaches that supreme divine Person.
Knowers of the Veda call it the imperishable. Ascetics free of passion enter it, and those who want it practice celibacy. I will tell you of that state briefly.
Close all the gates of the body, confine the mind in the heart, place the breath in the head, and stay established in yogic concentration.
Whoever departs this way, leaving the body while uttering Om, the one-syllabled brahman, and remembering me, goes to the supreme goal.
I am easy to reach, Pārtha, for the yogin who is always yoked and remembers me constantly, never thinking of anything else.
Having come to me, the great selves who have reached supreme perfection do not undergo birth again, that impermanent home of sorrow.
All worlds up to the realm of Brahmā are subject to return, Arjuna. But one who comes to me, son of Kuntī, is not reborn.
People who know that a day of Brahmā lasts a thousand ages [*yuga*], and that his night ends after a thousand ages, truly know day and night.
At the coming of his day, all manifest things arise from the unmanifest. At the coming of his night, they dissolve into that same unmanifest.
This same multitude of beings comes into being again and again. It dissolves helplessly at the coming of night, Pārtha, and arises again at the coming of day.
But beyond that unmanifest is another, eternal unmanifest being, which does not perish when all beings perish.
This unmanifest is called the imperishable, and they call it the supreme goal. Those who reach it do not return. That is my supreme abode.
That supreme Person, Pārtha, in whom beings abide and by whom all this is pervaded, can be reached by exclusive devotion [*bhakti*].
Now, bull of the Bhāratas, I will tell you the times at which departing yogins return or do not return.
Fire, light, day, the bright half of the month, the six months when the sun moves north: those who know brahman and depart then go to brahman.
Smoke, night, the dark half of the month, the six months when the sun moves south: the yogin who departs then reaches the light of the moon and returns.
These two paths, the bright and the dark, are held to be eternal for the world. By one, a person goes and does not return; by the other, a person returns again.
No yogin who knows these two paths is deluded, Pārtha. Therefore be yoked in yoga at all times, Arjuna.
Merit and its fruit are assigned to the Vedas, to sacrifices, austerities, and gifts. Knowing this teaching, the yogin goes beyond all of it and reaches the supreme, primal place.

chapters.title: The Yoga of the Royal Knowledge and the Royal Secret

verses.text: Since you do not find fault, I will declare to you this most secret knowledge together with discernment. Knowing it, you will be freed from evil.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: It is royal knowledge, a royal secret [*rāja-vidyā, rāja-guhya*]: the supreme purifier, directly seen, in accord with dharma, very easy to practice, and imperishable.
People without faith in this dharma, scorcher of foes, do not reach me. They return to the path of death and saṁsāra.
This whole world is pervaded by me in my unmanifest form. All beings abide in me, but I do not abide in them.
And yet beings do not abide in me. Behold my sovereign yoga! My self sustains beings and is their source, but it does not abide in them.
The great wind moves everywhere yet always abides in space. In the same way, understand that all beings abide in me.
At the end of a cosmic age [*kalpa*], son of Kuntī, all beings pass into my nature. At the beginning of a cosmic age I send them forth again.
Resting on my own nature, I send forth again and again this whole multitude of beings, which is helpless under the power of nature.
These actions do not bind me, Dhanañjaya. I sit as if indifferent, unattached to those actions.
With me as overseer, nature gives birth to the moving and the unmoving. For this reason, son of Kuntī, the world revolves.
The deluded despise me when I take on a human body. They do not know my higher being as the great lord of beings.
Their hopes, their actions, and their knowledge are vain, and they lack insight. They take on the deluding nature of fiends and demons.
But the great selves, Pārtha, rely on the divine nature. Knowing me as the imperishable source of beings, they worship me with minds that do not stray.
Always glorifying me, striving with firm vows, bowing to me with devotion, always yoked, they worship me.
Others worship me by offering the sacrifice of knowledge. They worship me as one, as distinct, and as manifold, facing in all directions.
I am the ritual; I am the sacrifice; I am the offering to the ancestors; I am the healing herb. I am the mantra; I am the clarified butter; I am the fire; I am the oblation.
I am the father of this world, its mother, its establisher, its grandfather. I am what is to be known, the purifier, the syllable Om, the Ṛg, the Sāman, and the Yajus.
I am the goal, the supporter, the lord, the witness, the dwelling, the refuge, the friend. I am the origin, the dissolution, the ground, the treasure-house, the imperishable seed.
I give heat; I hold back the rain and send it forth. I am immortality and death, being and non-being [*sat* and *asat*], Arjuna.

Knowers of the three Vedas, drinkers of soma purified of evil, worship me with sacrifices and pray for the way to heaven. They reach the pure world of the lord of the gods and enjoy in heaven the divine enjoyments of the gods.

Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world, they enter the world of mortals again when their merit is used up. So those who follow the dharma of the three Vedas, desiring desires, gain only coming and going.
But some people think of no other and worship me alone. They are always yoked, and for them I secure both gain and safekeeping [*yoga-kṣema*].
Even those who are devoted to other gods and sacrifice to them with faith are in fact sacrificing to me, son of Kuntī, though not according to the rule.
For I am the enjoyer and the lord of all sacrifices. But they do not recognize me in truth, and so they fall.
Those vowed to the gods go to the gods; those vowed to the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who sacrifice to spirits go to the spirits. Those who sacrifice to me come to me.
Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, I accept that offering of devotion from one whose self is pure.
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer, whatever you give, whatever austerity you perform, son of Kuntī, do it as an offering to me.
In this way you will be freed from the bonds of action and their good and evil fruits. With your self yoked in the yoga of renunciation, you will be freed and come to me.
I am the same toward all beings. No one is hateful to me, and no one is dear. But those who worship me with devotion are in me, and I am in them.
Even if someone of very bad conduct worships me with undivided devotion, that person should be considered good, for he has resolved rightly.
He quickly becomes a self of dharma and reaches lasting peace. Son of Kuntī, know for certain: my devotee does not perish.
For those who take refuge in me, Pārtha, even those of lowly birth [*pāpa-yonayaḥ*], and women, vaiśyas, and śūdras too, reach the supreme goal.
tnotes: The Sanskrit can be read in two ways. One makes "of lowly birth" a separate group. The other makes it a label for the women, vaiśyas, and śūdras that follow. Many modern readers take the first, more inclusive reading.

verses.text: How much more, then, pure brāhmaṇas and devoted royal seers! You have come into this impermanent, joyless world, so worship me.
Let your mind be on me; be devoted to me; sacrifice to me; bow down to me. Having yoked your self in this way, with me as your highest aim, you will come to me.

chapters.title: The Yoga of Divine Manifestations

verses.text: Once again, mighty-armed one, hear my supreme word. You take delight in it, and I will speak it to you because I wish for your good.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know my origin, for in every way I am the source of the gods and the great seers.
One who knows me as unborn and without beginning, the great lord of the world, is undeluded among mortals and freed from all evils.
Understanding, knowledge, freedom from delusion, patience, truth, self-restraint, calm, pleasure and pain, existence and non-existence, fear and fearlessness,
non-harming [*ahiṁsā*], equanimity, contentment, austerity, generosity, fame and infamy: these various states of beings come from me alone.
The seven great seers of old and the four Manus came from my mind and share my nature. From them come these creatures in the world.
One who knows in truth this extended power [*vibhūti*] and yoga of mine is yoked by unwavering yoga. Of this there is no doubt.
I am the origin of all, and from me everything proceeds. Knowing this, the wise worship me, filled with love [*bhāva*].
With their thoughts on me and their lives given to me, they enlighten one another and always speak of me. They are content and full of delight.
To those who are always yoked and worship me with love, I give the yoga of understanding by which they come to me.
Out of compassion for them, abiding in their own being, I destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.
You are the supreme brahman, the supreme abode, the supreme purifier: the eternal divine Person, the first god, unborn and all-pervading.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: So all the seers say of you, and the divine seer Nārada, Asita Devala, and Vyāsa. And you yourself tell me so.
I hold all that you tell me to be true, Keśava. Neither the gods nor the demons, Blessed One, know your manifestation.
You alone know yourself by yourself, Supreme Person: source of beings, lord of beings, god of gods, lord of the world.
Tell me fully of your divine extended powers, by which you pervade these worlds and abide in them.
How may I know you, yogin, through constant meditation? In what forms of being should I meditate on you, Blessed One?
Tell me again in detail of your yoga and extended power, Janārdana. I never tire of hearing your nectar.
Very well. I will tell you of my divine extended powers, best of Kurus, but only the principal ones, for there is no end to my extent.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: I am the self, Guḍākeśa, abiding in the heart of all beings. I am the beginning, the middle, and the end of beings.
Among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; among lights, the radiant sun. I am Marīci among the Maruts, and among the stars I am the moon.
Among the Vedas I am the Sāmaveda; among the gods, Indra. Among the senses I am the mind, and in beings I am consciousness [*cetanā*].
Among the Rudras I am Śaṅkara; among yakṣas and rākṣasas, Kubera, lord of wealth. Among the Vasus I am fire, and among mountains, Meru.
Among household priests, Pārtha, know me as the chief, Bṛhaspati. Among generals I am Skanda; among bodies of water, the ocean.
Among the great seers I am Bhṛgu; among utterances, the single syllable [Om]. Among sacrifices I am the sacrifice of murmured prayer [*japa*]; among immovable things, the Himālaya.
Among all trees I am the aśvattha [sacred fig]; among divine seers, Nārada. Among gandharvas I am Citraratha; among the perfected, the sage Kapila.
Among horses know me as Uccaiḥśravas, born of the nectar; among lordly elephants, Airāvata; and among men, the king.
Among weapons I am the thunderbolt; among cows, the wish-granting cow. I am Kandarpa [Love], who begets; among serpents I am Vāsuki.
Among nāgas I am Ananta; among water-beings, Varuṇa. Among the ancestors I am Aryaman; among those who restrain, Yama.
Among the daityas I am Prahlāda; among those who reckon, I am time. Among beasts I am the lion; among birds, Garuḍa, son of Vinatā.
Among purifiers I am the wind; among those who bear arms, Rāma. Among sea-creatures I am the makara; among rivers, the Gaṅgā.
Of creations I am the beginning, the end, and the middle, Arjuna. Among sciences I am the science of the self; in those who debate, I am the reasoning.
Among letters I am the letter A; among compounds, the copulative compound [*dvandva*]. I am imperishable time; I am the establisher, facing in all directions.
I am all-seizing death and the origin of all that is to come. Among feminine powers I am fame, fortune, speech, memory, intelligence, steadfastness, and patience.
tnotes: These seven nouns are feminine in Sanskrit, and each is also a goddess.

verses.text: Among chants I am the Bṛhat-sāman; among meters, the gāyatrī. Among months I am Mārgaśīrṣa; among seasons, the flowering spring.
I am the gambling of cheats and the splendor of the splendid. I am victory, I am resolve, I am the goodness [*sattva*] of the good.
Among the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva; among the Pāṇḍavas, Dhanañjaya. Among sages I am Vyāsa; among poets, the poet Uśanas.
I am the rod of those who punish and the statecraft of those who seek victory. I am the silence of secret things and the knowledge of those who know.
Whatever is the seed of all beings, that I am, Arjuna. No being, moving or unmoving, could exist without me.
There is no end to my divine extended powers, scorcher of foes. What I have said of their extent is only a set of examples.
Whatever being has power, splendor, or vigor, understand that it arises from a fraction of my brilliance.
But what use is all this detailed knowledge to you, Arjuna? I stand supporting this whole world with a single fraction of myself.

chapters.title: The Yoga of the Vision of the Universal Form

verses.text: As a favor to me, you have spoken the supreme secret called the inner self [*adhyātma*]. Through these words of yours my delusion is gone.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: For I have heard from you in detail, lotus-eyed one, of the arising and passing away of beings, and of your imperishable greatness.
It is just as you have described yourself, supreme lord. Now, Supreme Person, I wish to see your sovereign form.
If you think it possible for me to see it, Lord, lord of yoga, then show me your imperishable self.
Behold, Pārtha, my forms by the hundreds and thousands: various, divine, of many colors and shapes.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the Maruts. Behold many wonders never seen before, Bhārata.
Behold today the whole world, moving and unmoving, standing as one here in my body, Guḍākeśa, and whatever else you wish to see.
But you cannot see me with this eye of yours. I give you a divine eye. Behold my sovereign yoga!
Having spoken thus, O king, Hari, the great lord of yoga, showed Pārtha his supreme sovereign form.
verses.speaker: Sañjaya

verses.text: It had many mouths and eyes and many wondrous sights, many divine ornaments and many divine weapons raised.
It wore divine garlands and garments and was anointed with divine perfumes: the infinite god, all-wondrous, facing in all directions.
If the light of a thousand suns were to rise at once in the sky, it might be like the light of that great self.
There, in the body of the god of gods, Pāṇḍava saw the whole world, divided in many ways, standing as one.
Then Dhanañjaya, filled with amazement and with his hair standing on end, bowed his head to the god, joined his palms, and said:
O God, I see in your body the gods and all the hosts of beings: Brahmā the lord, seated on the lotus, and all the seers and divine serpents.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: I see you on every side, endless in form, with countless arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes. I see no end of you, no middle, and no beginning, lord of all, whose form is the universe.
I see you wearing a crown and bearing a mace and discus, a mass of brilliance shining everywhere. You are hard to look at, blazing on all sides like burning fire and sun, beyond measure.
You are the imperishable, the supreme thing to be known. You are the final resting place of all this. You are the undying guardian of eternal dharma. You are the ancient Person, I believe.
I see you without beginning, middle, or end, of infinite power and countless arms, with moon and sun as eyes and blazing fire as mouth, burning this whole world with your radiance.
The space between heaven and earth and all the directions are filled by you alone. Seeing this wondrous and terrible form of yours, great self, the three worlds tremble.
These hosts of gods enter into you. Some, terrified, praise you with joined palms. Crying "Hail!", the hosts of great seers and the perfected praise you with abundant hymns.
The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts, and the ancestors, and the hosts of gandharvas, yakṣas, asuras, and the perfected all gaze at you in amazement.
Your form is great, mighty-armed one, with many mouths and eyes, many arms, thighs, and feet, many bellies, terrible with many tusks. Seeing it, the worlds tremble, and so do I.
You touch the sky, blazing and many-colored, with gaping mouths and huge blazing eyes. Seeing you, Viṣṇu, my innermost self trembles, and I find no steadiness or peace.
Seeing your mouths, terrible with tusks, like the fire of time [*kāla*] at the world's end, I lose all sense of direction and find no refuge. Be gracious, lord of gods, home of the world!
And all these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with hosts of kings, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and that son of a charioteer [Karṇa], together with our own chief warriors,
are rushing into your terrible mouths with their fearsome tusks. Some are seen caught between your teeth, their heads crushed.
As the many rushing torrents of rivers race toward the ocean, so these heroes of the human world enter your blazing mouths.
As moths rush with great speed into a blazing fire to their destruction, so these worlds rush with great speed into your mouths to their destruction.
Devouring all the worlds on every side with your flaming mouths, you lick your lips. Your terrible rays fill the whole world with brilliance and scorch it, Viṣṇu.
Tell me who you are, with so terrible a form. Homage to you, best of gods; be gracious! I want to understand you, the primal one, for I do not understand what you are doing.
I am time [*kāla*], the mighty destroyer of worlds, set in motion here to annihilate the worlds. Even without you, all these warriors drawn up in the opposing ranks will cease to be.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Therefore stand up and win glory. Conquer your enemies and enjoy a prosperous kingdom. I have already slain them. Be merely the instrument [*nimitta-mātra*], left-handed archer.
Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Jayadratha, Karṇa, and the other heroic warriors are already slain by me. Kill them, and do not waver. Fight! You will conquer your rivals in battle.
Hearing these words of Keśava, the crowned one [Arjuna], trembling, joined his palms and bowed down. Overwhelmed with fear, he bowed again and spoke to Kṛṣṇa in a faltering voice:
verses.speaker: Sañjaya

verses.text: It is right, Hṛṣīkeśa, that the world rejoices and delights in praising you. The demons flee in terror in all directions, and all the hosts of the perfected bow down to you.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: And why should they not bow to you, great self? You are greater even than Brahmā, the first creator. Infinite lord of gods, home of the world, you are the imperishable: being and non-being, and what is beyond both.

You are the first god, the ancient Person, the supreme resting place of this world. You are the knower and what is to be known, and the supreme abode. The world is pervaded by you, whose form is infinite.
You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, and the moon; you are Prajāpati and the great-grandfather. Homage, homage to you a thousand times, and again and yet again homage to you!
Homage to you in front and behind, homage to you on every side, you who are all. Your valor is infinite and your might is immeasurable. You encompass everything, so you are everything.
I thought of you as a friend, and spoke rashly: "O Kṛṣṇa, O Yādava, O friend." I did not know this greatness of yours, and spoke from carelessness or from affection.
If I showed you disrespect in jest, at play, lying down, sitting, or eating, whether alone or before others, Acyuta, I ask forgiveness of you, the immeasurable one.

You are the father of the world, of all that moves and does not move. You are its object of worship and its most venerable teacher. No one equals you in the three worlds; how could anyone surpass you, whose power is beyond compare?
So I bow down and lay my body before you, and seek your grace, praiseworthy Lord. Bear with me, O God, as a father with a son, a friend with a friend, a lover with the beloved.
I am thrilled to have seen what was never seen before, yet my mind is shaken with fear. Show me that other form of yours, O God. Be gracious, lord of gods, home of the world.
I want to see you as before, wearing your crown, with mace and discus in hand. Take on that four-armed form, thousand-armed one, whose form is the universe.
By my grace, Arjuna, through my own yoga, I have shown you this supreme form. It is made of brilliance, universal, infinite, and primal, and no one but you has seen it before.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Not through the Vedas, sacrifices, or study, not through gifts or rites or fierce austerities, can anyone but you in the human world see me in this form, hero of the Kurus.
Do not be afraid or bewildered at seeing this terrible form of mine. Free of fear and with a glad mind, behold again this form of mine.
Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva showed his own form again. Taking on his gentle form once more, the great self consoled the frightened Arjuna.
verses.speaker: Sañjaya

verses.text: Seeing this gentle human form of yours, Janārdana, I am now composed and have returned to my own nature.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: This form of mine that you have seen is very hard to see. Even the gods always long to see it.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Not through the Vedas, austerity, gifts, or sacrifice can I be seen as you have seen me.
But through undivided devotion, Arjuna, I can be known in this way, seen in truth, and entered, scorcher of foes.
One who does my work, who holds me as highest, who is devoted to me, free of attachment and without hostility toward any being, comes to me, Pāṇḍava.

chapters.title: The Yoga of Devotion

verses.text: Some devotees, always yoked, worship you in this way. Others worship the imperishable, the unmanifest. Which of these know yoga better?
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: Those who fix their minds on me and worship me, always yoked and endowed with supreme faith, I consider the most fully yoked.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: But there are also those who worship the imperishable, which cannot be defined: the unmanifest, all-pervading and unthinkable, unchanging [*kūṭa-stha*], unmoving and constant.
They restrain all the senses, are equal-minded toward everything, and delight in the welfare of all beings. They too reach me.
The struggle is greater for those whose thought is fixed on the unmanifest, for the goal of the unmanifest is hard for the embodied to reach.
But others surrender all actions in me and are intent on me. They meditate on me and worship me with undivided yoga.
Their thought has entered into me, Pārtha, and I soon become their deliverer from the ocean of death and saṁsāra.
Place your mind in me alone, and let your understanding enter into me. From then on you will dwell in me alone. Of this there is no doubt.
But if you cannot fix your thought firmly on me, then seek to reach me through the yoga of practice, Dhanañjaya.
If you are not capable even of practice, devote yourself to doing work for my sake. Even by doing actions for my sake you will reach perfection.
If you cannot do even this, then rely on my yoga, control yourself, and give up the fruit of all actions.
Knowledge is better than practice. Meditation is better than knowledge. Giving up the fruit of action is better than meditation, and from giving it up, peace follows at once.
One who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, without "mine" and without I-making, the same in pain and pleasure, and patient,
always content, a yogin, self-controlled and firm in resolve, with mind and understanding offered to me: that devotee of mine is dear to me.
One from whom the world does not shrink and who does not shrink from the world, free from elation, impatience, fear, and agitation, is dear to me.
One who expects nothing, who is pure and capable, impartial and free of anxiety, who has given up all ambitious undertakings: that devotee of mine is dear to me.
One who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, who has given up both good and bad and is full of devotion, is dear to me.
One who is the same toward enemy and friend, in honor and dishonor, the same in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, free from attachment,
who treats blame and praise alike, who is silent and content with whatever comes, without a fixed home, steady-minded, and full of devotion: that person is dear to me.
But those devotees who, full of faith and holding me as highest, follow this nectar of dharma as I have taught it are exceedingly dear to me.

chapters.title: The Yoga of the Field and the Knower of the Field

verses.text: This body, son of Kuntī, is called the field [*kṣetra*]. Those who know it call the one who knows it the knower of the field [*kṣetrajña*].
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Know that I am the knower of the field in all fields, Bhārata. Knowledge of the field and of the knower of the field is what I hold to be true knowledge.
Hear from me briefly what the field is and what it is like, what its changes are and where it comes from, and who the knower is and what powers he has.
Seers have sung of this in many ways and in various distinct hymns, and in the reasoned, conclusive words of the Brahma-sūtras.
The great elements, I-making, understanding, and the unmanifest; the ten senses and the one [the mind]; the five domains of the senses;
desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the bodily whole, awareness, and steadfastness: this, in brief, is the field with its changes.
Absence of pride, absence of deceit, non-harming, patience, uprightness, service to the teacher, purity, steadiness, self-restraint;
dispassion toward sense objects, absence of I-making, seeing clearly the evil of birth, death, old age, sickness, and pain;
non-attachment, not clinging to son, wife, home, and the like, and constant evenness of mind whether the wanted or the unwanted comes;
unwavering devotion to me through undivided yoga, resort to solitary places, distaste for crowds;
constancy in knowledge of the inner self, and insight into the aim of the knowledge of truth: this is called knowledge. What is contrary to it is ignorance.
I will declare what is to be known, knowing which one reaches immortality: the beginningless supreme brahman, which is said to be neither being nor non-being.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and mouths everywhere, with ears everywhere, it stands enveloping everything in the world.
It seems to have the qualities of all the senses, yet it is free of all the senses. It is unattached, yet it supports all. It is free of the guṇas, yet it experiences the guṇas.
It is outside and inside beings, unmoving and moving. It is too subtle to be known. It is far away, and it is near.
It is undivided, yet it seems to be divided among beings. It is to be known as the one who sustains beings, devours them, and brings them forth.
It is the light of lights, said to be beyond darkness. It is knowledge, what is to be known, and what knowledge reaches, seated in the heart of all.
So the field, knowledge, and what is to be known have been briefly described. My devotee who understands this enters into my state of being.
Know that nature [*prakṛti*] and person [*puruṣa*] are both beginningless, and that the changes and the guṇas arise from nature.
Nature is said to be the cause of effect, instrument, and agency. The person is said to be the cause of the experience of pleasure and pain.
For the person, situated in nature, experiences the guṇas born of nature. Attachment to the guṇas causes its births in good and evil wombs.
The supreme person in this body is called the witness, the one who consents, the supporter, the experiencer, the great lord, and the supreme self.
One who knows the person, and nature together with the guṇas, in this way is not born again, however one may live.
Some see the self in the self by the self through meditation; others through the yoga of Sāṅkhya; and others through the yoga of action.
Yet others, not knowing this, hear it from others and worship. Devoted to what they have heard, they too cross beyond death.
Whatever being comes into existence, moving or unmoving, know, bull of the Bhāratas, that it arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field.
One who sees the supreme lord abiding equally in all beings, not perishing when they perish, truly sees.
Seeing the same lord established everywhere, one does not harm the self by the self, and so goes to the supreme goal.
One who sees that all actions are done by nature alone, and that the self is therefore not the doer, truly sees.
When one sees the separate existence of beings as resting in the One, and their unfolding from that One alone, one reaches brahman.
Because it is beginningless and free of the guṇas, this imperishable supreme self neither acts nor is tainted, son of Kuntī, even though it dwells in the body.
Space pervades everything yet is not tainted, because it is so subtle. In the same way the self, dwelling everywhere in the body, is not tainted.
As the one sun lights up this whole world, so the lord of the field lights up the whole field, Bhārata.
Those who, with the eye of knowledge, know this difference between the field and the knower of the field, and know the release of beings from nature, go to the supreme.
tnotes: Some manuscripts open this chapter with an extra verse (Arjuna's question about nature, person, field, and knower), which would make it 35 verses. The standard numbering, used here, leaves that verse out.
