chapters.title: The Yoga of the Three Guṇas

verses.text: I will declare again the supreme knowledge, the highest of all knowledge. Knowing it, all the sages have gone from here to supreme perfection.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Relying on this knowledge, they have come to share my nature. They are not born at the creation of the world, and they are not disturbed at its dissolution.
My womb is the great brahman [here, primal nature]. In it I place the seed, and from that, Bhārata, all beings come to be.
Whatever forms arise in any womb, son of Kuntī, the great brahman is their womb, and I am the father who gives the seed.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas, the guṇas born of nature, bind the imperishable embodied one in the body, mighty-armed one.
Of these, sattva is stainless, so it gives light and is free of disorder. It binds by attachment to happiness and attachment to knowledge, sinless one.
Know that rajas is passion in nature, arising from craving and attachment. It binds the embodied one, son of Kuntī, by attachment to action.
But know that tamas is born of ignorance and deludes all embodied beings. It binds by negligence, laziness, and sleep, Bhārata.
Sattva attaches one to happiness and rajas to action, Bhārata. But tamas covers knowledge and attaches one to negligence.
Sattva arises by overpowering rajas and tamas, Bhārata. Rajas arises by overpowering sattva and tamas. In the same way, tamas arises by overpowering sattva and rajas.
When the light of knowledge shines through all the gates of this body, then know that sattva has grown strong.
Greed, activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness, and longing arise when rajas has grown strong, bull of the Bhāratas.
Darkness, inactivity, negligence, and delusion arise when tamas has grown strong, joy of the Kurus.
When the embodied one dies while sattva prevails, it reaches the stainless worlds of those who know the highest.
Dying in rajas, one is born among those attached to action. Dying in tamas, one is born in the wombs of the deluded.
The fruit of good action is said to be pure and of the nature of sattva. The fruit of rajas is pain, and the fruit of tamas is ignorance.
Knowledge arises from sattva and greed from rajas. Negligence and delusion arise from tamas, and ignorance too.
Those established in sattva go upward. Those of rajas stay in the middle. Those of tamas, living by the lowest guṇa, go downward.
When the seer sees no doer other than the guṇas and knows what is beyond the guṇas, he comes to my state of being.
Going beyond these three guṇas, from which the body arises, the embodied one is freed from birth, death, old age, and sorrow, and reaches immortality.
By what marks, Lord, is one known who has gone beyond these three guṇas? How does that person live, and how does he go beyond the three guṇas?
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: One who does not hate light, activity, or delusion when they arise, Pāṇḍava, and does not long for them when they cease;
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: who sits as if indifferent and is not disturbed by the guṇas; who knows "it is only the guṇas moving" and stands firm without wavering;

who is the same in pain and pleasure, abiding in the self, to whom a clod, a stone, and gold are the same; who is equal toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, steadfast, equal toward blame and praise;
who is equal in honor and dishonor, equal toward friend and foe, and has given up all ambitious undertakings: that one is said to have gone beyond the guṇas.
And one who serves me with the unwavering yoga of devotion goes beyond these guṇas and is fit to become brahman.
For I am the foundation [*pratiṣṭhā*] of brahman, of the immortal and imperishable, of eternal dharma, and of absolute happiness.

chapters.title: The Yoga of the Supreme Person

verses.text: They speak of an imperishable aśvattha tree with its roots above and its branches below. Its leaves are the Vedic hymns. One who knows it knows the Veda.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Its branches spread below and above, nourished by the guṇas, with sense objects as their shoots. And below, its roots stretch out, binding people to action in the human world.
Its form cannot be perceived here, nor its end, nor its beginning, nor its foundation. Cut down this firmly rooted aśvattha with the strong axe of non-attachment.
Then seek that place from which those who go there never return, thinking: "I take refuge in that primal Person from whom the ancient stream of activity flowed forth."

Without pride or delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, always devoted to the inner self, with desires turned away and freed from the pairs called pleasure and pain, the undeluded go to that imperishable place.
Neither sun nor moon nor fire lights it. Those who go there do not return. That is my supreme abode.
A fragment of me, becoming an eternal living being [*jīva*] in the world of the living, draws to itself the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which rest in nature.
When the lord takes on a body and when he leaves it, he takes these with him and goes, as the wind carries scents from their sources.
Presiding over hearing, sight, touch, taste, and smell, and over the mind, he enjoys the objects of the senses.
The deluded do not see him departing, staying, or enjoying, joined with the guṇas. Those with the eye of knowledge see him.
Yogins who strive see him established in themselves. But those whose selves are unformed and who lack insight do not see him, even when they strive.
The brilliance in the sun that lights up the whole world, the brilliance in the moon and in fire: know that this brilliance is mine.
Entering the earth, I sustain beings with my vigor. Becoming soma, the essence of sap, I nourish all plants.
Becoming the digestive fire, I dwell in the bodies of living beings. Joined with the in-breath and out-breath, I digest the four kinds of food.
I am seated in the heart of all. From me come memory and knowledge, and their loss. I am what is to be known through all the Vedas. I am the maker of the Vedānta, and I am the knower of the Veda.
There are two persons in this world: the perishable [*kṣara*] and the imperishable [*akṣara*]. The perishable is all beings. The imperishable is called the unchanging one [*kūṭa-stha*].
But there is another, the highest person, called the supreme self. As the imperishable lord, he enters the three worlds and sustains them.
Because I am beyond the perishable and higher even than the imperishable, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person [*puruṣottama*].
One who is undeluded and knows me in this way as the Supreme Person knows all, and worships me with one's whole being, Bhārata.
So I have declared this most secret teaching, sinless one. Understanding it, one becomes wise and has done all that needs to be done, Bhārata.

chapters.title: The Yoga of the Divine and Demonic Endowments

verses.text: Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, generosity, self-restraint, sacrifice, study of scripture, austerity, uprightness;
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: non-harming, truth, freedom from anger, renunciation, peace, refraining from slander, compassion for beings, freedom from greed, gentleness, modesty, steadiness;
vigor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, freedom from malice, and freedom from arrogance: these belong to one born to the divine endowment [*daivī sampad*], Bhārata.
Hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance belong to one born to the demonic endowment [*āsurī sampad*], Pārtha.
The divine endowment is held to lead to liberation, and the demonic to bondage. Do not grieve, Pāṇḍava. You are born to the divine endowment.
There are two kinds of beings created in this world, the divine and the demonic. I have described the divine at length. Now hear from me about the demonic, Pārtha.
Demonic people do not know when to act and when to refrain. Neither purity nor good conduct nor truth is found in them.
They say the world is without truth, without foundation, and without a lord. They say it does not come from any chain of causes, but from desire alone. What else, they ask, could cause it?
Holding this view, these lost selves of small understanding and cruel deeds rise up as enemies to destroy the world.
Relying on desire that can never be satisfied, full of hypocrisy, pride, and intoxication, they take up false notions through delusion and act on impure vows.
They cling to boundless anxiety that ends only with death. They hold the enjoyment of desires as the highest aim and are sure that this is all there is.
Bound by hundreds of ties of hope and given over to desire and anger, they seek to pile up wealth by unjust means to enjoy their desires.
"This I have gained today; this wish I will fulfill. This is mine, and this wealth too will be mine.
I have killed that enemy, and I will kill others too. I am the lord, I am the enjoyer. I am successful, strong, and happy.
I am rich and well-born. Who else is like me? I will sacrifice, I will give, I will rejoice." So they think, deluded by ignorance.
Bewildered by many thoughts, caught in the net of delusion, attached to the enjoyment of desires, they fall into a foul hell.
Full of self-regard and stubborn, filled with the pride and intoxication of wealth, they offer sacrifices in name only, with hypocrisy and not according to the rule.
Given to I-making, force, arrogance, desire, and anger, these envious ones hate me, who dwell in their own bodies and in the bodies of others.
These hateful, cruel, vile, inauspicious lowest of humans I hurl again and again, through the cycles of rebirth, into demonic wombs.
Entering demonic wombs, deluded birth after birth and never reaching me, son of Kuntī, they go to the lowest state.
This is the threefold gate of hell, which destroys the self: desire, anger, and greed. Therefore one should give up these three.
A person released from these three gates of darkness, son of Kuntī, does what is good for the self and then goes to the supreme goal.
One who casts aside the rule of scripture [*śāstra*] and acts on the impulse of desire reaches neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.
So let scripture be your standard in deciding what should and should not be done. Knowing what the rule of scripture says, you should do your work here.

chapters.title: The Yoga of the Three Kinds of Faith

verses.text: Some people set aside the rule of scripture yet sacrifice with faith. What is their standing, Kṛṣṇa? Is it sattva, rajas, or tamas?
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: The faith of embodied beings is of three kinds, born of their own nature: of sattva, of rajas, and of tamas. Hear about it.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Each person's faith follows his inner being [*sattva*], Bhārata. A person is made of faith: whatever one's faith is, that is what one is.
People of sattva worship the gods. People of rajas worship yakṣas and rākṣasas. The others, people of tamas, worship ghosts and hosts of spirits.
Some people practice terrible austerities that scripture does not prescribe. They are full of hypocrisy and I-making, driven by the force of desire and passion.
Senseless, they torment the elements that make up the body, and me as well, who dwell within the body. Know that their resolve is demonic.
The food that each person likes is also of three kinds, and so are sacrifice, austerity, and giving. Hear how they differ.
Foods that increase life, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and satisfaction, foods that are savory, smooth, nourishing, and pleasing to the heart, are dear to people of sattva.
Foods that are bitter, sour, salty, very hot, pungent, harsh, and burning, and that cause pain, grief, and sickness, are desired by people of rajas.
Food that is stale, tasteless, putrid, and spoiled, leftover and impure, is dear to people of tamas.
Sacrifice is of sattva when it is offered according to the rule by those who do not want its fruit, with the mind fixed only on the thought "this ought to be offered."
But sacrifice offered with an eye to its fruit, or for show, best of Bhāratas, know to be of rajas.
Sacrifice that ignores the rule, in which no food is shared, no mantras are spoken, no priests are paid, and there is no faith, is called of tamas.
Reverence for the gods, the twice-born, teachers, and the wise; purity, uprightness, celibacy, and non-harming are called austerity of the body.
Speech that does not cause distress, that is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial, and regular recitation of scripture are called austerity of speech.
Calm of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint, and purity of being are called austerity of the mind.
When yoked people practice this threefold austerity with supreme faith and without wanting its fruit, it is called of sattva.
Austerity practiced to gain respect, honor, and reverence, or out of hypocrisy, is called of rajas. It is unstable and does not last.
Austerity practiced from a deluded idea, by torturing oneself, or to ruin another, is called of tamas.
A gift is held to be of sattva when it is given because it ought to be given, to one who cannot repay, at the right place and time, to a worthy person.
But a gift given to get something back, or with an eye to its fruit, or given grudgingly, is held to be of rajas.
A gift given at the wrong place and time, to the unworthy, without respect and with contempt, is called of tamas.
"Om tat sat": this is held to be the threefold name of brahman. By it, the brāhmaṇas, the Vedas, and sacrifices were established long ago.
That is why those who teach brahman always begin the acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity prescribed by the rule with the word "Om."
With the word "tat" ["that"], seekers of liberation perform acts of sacrifice and austerity and various acts of giving without aiming at the fruit.
"Sat" is used to mean reality and goodness. In the same way, Pārtha, the word "sat" is used for any praiseworthy act.
Steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity, and giving is also called "sat," and so is any action done for their sake.
Whatever is offered, given, or done as austerity without faith is called "asat," Pārtha. It counts for nothing, either here or hereafter.

chapters.title: The Yoga of Liberation through Renunciation

verses.text: Mighty-armed one, Hṛṣīkeśa, slayer of Keśin, I wish to know the truth about renunciation [*saṁnyāsa*] and about relinquishment [*tyāga*], each on its own.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: The wise understand renunciation as giving up actions done from desire. The discerning call giving up the fruit of all actions relinquishment.
verses.speaker: The Blessed Lord

verses.text: Some thinkers say that action should be relinquished because it is full of fault. Others say that acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity should not be relinquished.
Hear my conclusion about relinquishment, best of Bhāratas. Relinquishment, tiger among men, is said to be of three kinds.
Acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity should not be relinquished. They should be performed, for sacrifice, giving, and austerity purify the wise.
But even these actions should be performed without attachment and without seeking their fruit. This, Pārtha, is my settled and highest view.
It is not right to renounce prescribed action. Giving it up out of delusion is said to be of tamas.
One who gives up action because it is painful, from fear of bodily hardship, makes a relinquishment of rajas and does not gain the fruit of relinquishment.
When prescribed action is done simply because it ought to be done, Arjuna, without attachment and without seeking its fruit, that relinquishment is held to be of sattva.
The one who relinquishes in this way, filled with sattva, wise, and with doubts cut away, does not hate unpleasant action or cling to pleasant action.
No embodied being can give up actions entirely. But one who gives up the fruit of action is called a relinquisher.
For those who have not relinquished, the fruit of action after death is threefold: unwanted, wanted, and mixed. For renunciants there is none at all.
Learn from me, mighty-armed one, the five factors that bring about every action, as taught in the Sāṅkhya doctrine:
the basis [the body], the agent, the various instruments, the various distinct activities, and fifth, the divine [*daiva*, fate or providence].
tnotes: *daiva* can mean the gods, unseen causes, fate, or providence. The Gītā does not settle which.

verses.text: Whatever action a person undertakes with body, speech, or mind, right or wrong, these five are its causes.
That being so, one who, through an unformed understanding, sees the self alone as the agent does not truly see. That person's mind is perverse.
One who is free from the sense of I-making and whose understanding is untainted does not kill and is not bound, even if he kills these people.
Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower are the three things that prompt action. The instrument, the act, and the agent are the three parts of action.
In the doctrine of the guṇas, knowledge, action, and agent are each said to be of three kinds, according to the guṇas. Hear about these as well.
Knowledge of sattva is the knowledge by which one sees one imperishable being in all beings, undivided within the divided.
Knowledge of rajas sees in all beings many separate entities of different kinds.
Knowledge of tamas clings to one single thing as if it were the whole. It is without reason, does not grasp the truth, and is narrow.
Action of sattva is prescribed action, done without attachment, without passion or hatred, by one who does not want its fruit.
Action of rajas is done by one who wants to fulfill desires, or out of I-making, with great strain.
Action of tamas is undertaken through delusion, with no regard for consequences, loss, harm to others, or one's own ability.
The agent of sattva is free of attachment and does not talk about himself, is full of steadfastness and energy, and is unchanged in success and failure.
The agent of rajas is passionate and wants the fruit of action. He is greedy, violent, impure, and swings between elation and grief.
The agent of tamas is unyoked, crude, stubborn, deceitful, spiteful, lazy, despondent, and always putting things off.
Now hear, Dhanañjaya, the threefold division of understanding and of steadfastness [*dhṛti*] according to the guṇas, explained fully and one by one.
Understanding of sattva, Pārtha, knows when to engage and when to withdraw, what should and should not be done, what to fear and what not to fear, and what is bondage and what is liberation.
Understanding of rajas, Pārtha, misjudges dharma and adharma, and what should and should not be done.
Understanding of tamas, Pārtha, is covered by darkness. It takes adharma for dharma and sees all things upside down.
Steadfastness of sattva, Pārtha, holds steady the workings of mind, breath, and senses through unwavering yoga.
Steadfastness of rajas, Arjuna, holds to dharma, pleasure [*kāma*], and wealth [*artha*] out of attachment and desire for their fruit.
Steadfastness of tamas, Pārtha, is that by which the foolish will not let go of sleep, fear, grief, despondency, and arrogance.
Now hear from me, bull of the Bhāratas, about the three kinds of happiness. In one of them a person comes to delight through practice and reaches the end of sorrow.
Happiness of sattva is like poison at first and like nectar in the end. It is born of the clarity of one's own understanding.
Happiness of rajas arises from the meeting of the senses and their objects. It is like nectar at first and like poison in the end.
Happiness of tamas deludes the self both at first and in the end. It arises from sleep, laziness, and negligence.
There is no being on earth, or among the gods in heaven, that is free of these three guṇas born of nature.
The actions of brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, scorcher of foes, are divided according to the guṇas that arise from their own nature [*svabhāva*].
Calm, self-restraint, austerity, purity, patience, uprightness, knowledge, discernment, and faith are the action of the brāhmaṇa, born of his own nature.
Heroism, vigor, steadfastness, skill, not fleeing in battle, generosity, and leadership are the action of the kṣatriya, born of his own nature.
Farming, herding, and trade are the action of the vaiśya, born of his own nature. Action that consists of service is the action of the śūdra, born of his own nature.
Each person who delights in his own action reaches perfection. Hear how one devoted to one's own action finds perfection.
By worshiping, through one's own action, that from which beings arise and by which all this is pervaded, a person finds perfection.
Better one's own dharma, though imperfect, than another's dharma well performed. One who does the action set by one's own nature incurs no fault.
One should not give up the action one is born to, son of Kuntī, even if it is flawed. All undertakings are clouded by flaws, as fire is by smoke.
With understanding unattached everywhere, self-conquered and free of longing, one reaches through renunciation the supreme perfection of freedom from action [*naiṣkarmya-siddhi*].
Learn from me briefly, son of Kuntī, how one who has reached perfection reaches brahman, the highest culmination of knowledge.
Yoked with purified understanding, controlling the self with steadfastness, turning away from sound and the other objects of sense, setting aside attraction and aversion,
living in solitude, eating lightly, restraining speech, body, and mind, always intent on the yoga of meditation, relying on dispassion,
and letting go of I-making, force, arrogance, desire, anger, and possessiveness, without "mine" and at peace, one is fit to become brahman.
Having become brahman, serene in self, one neither grieves nor desires. Being the same toward all beings, one reaches supreme devotion to me.
Through devotion one knows me in truth: how great I am and who I am. Then, knowing me in truth, one enters into me at once.
Though always performing all kinds of actions, one who takes refuge in me reaches by my grace the eternal, imperishable abode.
In your mind surrender all actions to me. Hold me as highest, rely on the yoga of understanding, and keep your thought always on me.
With your thought on me, you will cross every obstacle by my grace. But if from I-making you will not listen, you will perish.
If you rely on I-making and think "I will not fight," your resolve is in vain. Your own nature will compel you.
You are bound, son of Kuntī, by your own action, born of your own nature. What you do not wish to do out of delusion, you will do even against your will.
The Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, Arjuna. By his māyā he makes all beings revolve, as if mounted on a machine.
Take refuge in him alone with your whole being, Bhārata. By his grace you will reach supreme peace and the eternal abode.
So I have declared to you knowledge more secret than any secret. Reflect on it fully, then do as you wish.
Hear again my supreme word, the most secret of all. You are deeply loved by me, so I will tell you what is good for you.
Let your mind be on me; be devoted to me; sacrifice to me; bow down to me. You will come to me. I promise you truly, for you are dear to me.
Abandon all dharmas and take refuge in me alone. I will free you from all evils. Do not grieve.
tnotes: This is the "final verse" (*carama-śloka*) for many traditions. "Abandon all dharmas" has been read as giving up attachment to the results of one's duties, giving up reliance on one's own efforts, or giving up all religious means in favor of grace. The Sanskrit allows each reading.

verses.text: You should never tell this to one without austerity, or without devotion, or to one who does not wish to listen, or to one who speaks ill of me.
One who teaches this supreme secret to my devotees, having shown the highest devotion to me, will come to me without doubt.
No one among humans does anything dearer to me than that person, and no one on earth will be dearer to me.
One who studies this dialogue of ours on dharma will have worshiped me with the sacrifice of knowledge. This is my view.
And a person who listens to it with faith and without finding fault will also be freed and will reach the auspicious worlds of those whose deeds are good.
Have you listened to this, Pārtha, with one-pointed thought? Has your delusion born of ignorance been destroyed, Dhanañjaya?
My delusion is destroyed, and through your grace, Acyuta, I have regained my memory [*smṛti*]. I stand firm, my doubts gone. I will do as you say.
verses.speaker: Arjuna

verses.text: So I have heard this wondrous dialogue between Vāsudeva and the great-souled Pārtha, which makes my hair stand on end.
verses.speaker: Sañjaya

verses.text: By the grace of Vyāsa I heard this supreme secret, this yoga, from Kṛṣṇa himself, the lord of yoga, as he declared it in person.
O king, as I remember again and again this wondrous and holy dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna, I rejoice again and again.
And as I remember again and again that most wondrous form of Hari, great is my amazement, O king, and I rejoice again and again.
Wherever there is Kṛṣṇa, the lord of yoga, and wherever there is Pārtha, the archer, there, I believe, are fortune, victory, prosperity, and sound policy [*nīti*].

chapters.colophon: Thus, in the Upaniṣads of the Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of brahman, the scripture of yoga, the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, ends the eighteenth chapter, called “The Yoga of Liberation through Renunciation.”

glossary.short: Kashmiri philosopher (c. 950–1016) who commented on the Kashmir recension of the Gītā from a non-dual Śaiva standpoint.
body: His *Gītārtha-saṅgraha* reads the text through Tantric non-dualism. It shows that the Gītā mattered beyond the Vaiṣṇava fold.

glossary.short: Practice: repeated, sustained effort that trains the mind.
body: "The mind is held by practice and dispassion" {6.35}. The same pair appears in *Yoga-sūtra* 1.12.

glossary.short: The breakdown of right order; lawlessness, injustice, the opposite of dharma.
body: Adharma is not simply individual wrongdoing but the systemic collapse of order. Arjuna fears it will follow the destruction of families {1.40}. Kṛṣṇa says he takes birth "whenever there is a decline of dharma and a rise of adharma" {4.7}. The understanding darkened by tamas "takes adharma for dharma" {18.32}: moral perception itself can be inverted.

glossary.short: The "pertaining to" series: what pertains to the self, to beings, to the gods, and to sacrifice (7.29–8.4).
body: These categories come from Upaniṣadic correspondences between the individual (*adhyātma*), the cosmos (*adhibhūta*), the divine (*adhidaiva*) and ritual (*adhiyajña*). Arjuna asks for definitions {8.1–2}. Kṛṣṇa answers that he himself is the principle of sacrifice "here in the body" {8.4}.

glossary.short: Non-dual Vedānta: the self is identical with brahman; the world of difference is appearance.
body: Śaṅkara's school. For Advaita the Gītā's final teaching is knowledge of the self as brahman. Karma-yoga purifies the mind but does not itself liberate.

glossary.short: "I-making": the ego-sense that says "I am the doer" and "this is mine."
body: A Sāṅkhya technical term: the evolute of nature that appropriates experience to a self. The translation renders it literally as "I-making" to keep its constructive sense. One "deluded by I-making thinks: 'I am the doer'" {3.27}. Freedom from it changes the moral status of even terrible acts {18.17}, one of the most debated claims in the text.

glossary.short: Non-harming: refraining from injury to any being.
body: The Gītā lists ahiṁsā among the divine qualities while urging Arjuna to fight. Gandhi resolved the tension by reading the war as allegory. Others accept it as the tension of a warrior ethic: violence that is just, dispassionate, and a last resort.

glossary.short: The imperishable: the undying reality; also "syllable," above all the syllable Om.
body: The word means both "indestructible" and "syllable," and the Gītā plays on both. Brahman is the supreme *akṣara* {8.3}, and Om is the "one-syllabled brahman" {8.13}. In {15.16–18} the imperishable is surpassed by the Supreme Person.

glossary.short: Third of the Pāṇḍava brothers, peerless archer, friend of Kṛṣṇa, the Gītā's questioner.
body: "Arjuna" means "bright, white." He is the epic's model warrior and the son of Indra. His collapse on the battlefield is the occasion of the Gītā. That such a hero breaks down makes the question universal: if Arjuna cannot act, who can?

glossary.short: The stages of life: student, householder, forest-dweller, renunciant.
body: Not named in the Gītā but presupposed. The text's argument with renunciation is partly an argument about whether liberation requires leaving the householder stage.

glossary.short: The sacred fig tree; in 15.1–3, the inverted tree of saṁsāra, roots above and branches below.
body: The image comes from *Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 6.1. The world grows down from its source. Its leaves are Vedic hymns, its shoots are sense objects, and it must be cut down with the axe of non-attachment.

glossary.short: The self: the conscious, unchanging core of a person. Also simply the reflexive "oneself."
body: The same word serves as the ordinary reflexive pronoun and as the metaphysical Self. The Gītā exploits the double sense: "lift up the self by the self" {6.5}. The self is unborn and undying {2.20}, beyond weapons and fire {2.23}, the witness of all {13.22}. For Advaita Vedānta ātman is identical with brahman. For Rāmānuja the self is a real, eternal mode of God. For Madhva it is eternally distinct from God.

glossary.short: "Taking oneself as the measure": seeing others' pleasure and pain as one's own (6.32).
body: The Gītā's version of the golden rule, rooted in the metaphysics of one self in all {6.29}.

glossary.short: Sri Aurobindo (1872–1950), revolutionary turned philosopher; his Essays on the Gita read it as a synthesis of works, knowledge and love.
"Descent": God's taking birth in the world to restore dharma.
body: The word itself does not occur in the Gītā, but {4.7–8} is its classic charter. "Whenever dharma declines… I come into being age after age." The verses ground the later doctrine of Viṣṇu's ten (or more) descents.

glossary.short: The unmanifest: what has not yet taken form; primal nature, or the formless absolute.
body: The word has two senses. One is cosmological: primal matter from which beings arise at Brahmā's dawn {8.18}. The other is metaphysical: the eternal unmanifest beyond that {8.20}. Chapter 12 weighs worship of the unmanifest against worship of the personal God.

glossary.short: "The Blessed One," the Lord: Kṛṣṇa's title as speaker; the God who possesses all excellences (bhaga).
body: *Bhaga* means fortune, share, excellence. The Bhagavat is the one who possesses them. The title gives the text its name, *Bhagavad-gītā*, "the song of the Blessed One." Traditions devoted to Bhagavān (Bhāgavatas, Pāñcarātra) formed the Gītā's early religious context.

glossary.short: The great devotional Purāṇa (c. 9th–10th century) narrating Kṛṣṇa's life, central to later Kṛṣṇa devotion.
Devotion: loving participation in God; from the root bhaj, "to share, partake."
body: The root *bhaj* means "to share in." Bhakti is not mere emotion but participation, a relation in which God also "shares himself" with the devotee {4.11}. The Gītā is among the earliest texts to make loving devotion to a personal God a full path to liberation. "Through devotion one knows me in truth" {18.55}. It was decisive for the later bhakti movements across India.

glossary.short: The discipline of devotion; title of Chapter 12.
body: Chapter 12 offers a graded ladder: fix the mind on God. If you cannot, practice. If not that, work for God. If not even that, give up the fruits of action {12.8–11}. The path accommodates every capacity.

glossary.short: The great-uncle of both parties, commander of the Kaurava army, bound by a vow of lifelong celibacy.
body: The revered elder whom Arjuna cannot bear to kill {2.4}. He fights for the side he knows to be wrong out of loyalty to the throne. He embodies the tragedy of conflicting duties.

glossary.short: The creator god, seated on the lotus; his day and night measure cosmic time.
body: A personal deity within the cosmos, not the absolute (*brahman*). Even "all worlds up to the realm of Brahmā" are subject to return {8.16}. Arjuna sees Brahmā within Kṛṣṇa's body {11.15}.

glossary.short: The "blowing-out in brahman": final peace and liberation.
body: *Nirvāṇa*, "extinction" like a flame blown out, is the Buddhist word for liberation. The Gītā's compound "nirvāṇa of brahman" is often read as a deliberate dialogue with Buddhism. It accepts the ideal of extinguished craving but grounds it in a positive absolute rather than in emptiness or cessation.

glossary.short: Bādarāyaṇa's aphorisms systematizing the Upaniṣads; one of Vedānta's three foundations.
body: {13.4} mentions "the words of the Brahma-sūtras." Whether this refers to Bādarāyaṇa's text, perhaps later than the Gītā, or to Upaniṣadic statements about brahman is debated.

glossary.short: The absolute: the ultimate ground of all that is; also the Veda, sacred utterance, and primal nature.
body: Originally the power of sacred speech in the Vedic hymns, then the Upaniṣadic absolute. The Gītā uses it in several senses. It is the supreme imperishable {8.3}, "neither being nor non-being" {13.12}. It is also the Veda {3.15} and the great womb of nature {14.3}. Strikingly, Kṛṣṇa calls himself "the foundation of brahman" {14.27}. This verse is pivotal for theistic readings in which the personal God exceeds the impersonal absolute. Do not confuse it with Brahmā, the creator god.

glossary.short: Member of the priestly and learned order; also a Vedic ritual text (the Brāhmaṇas).
body: The Gītā's ideal brāhmaṇa is marked by calm, self-restraint, austerity and knowledge {18.42}. The wise see "the same" in a learned brāhmaṇa and an outcaste {5.18}.

glossary.short: The two paths of the dead: the bright path of no return and the dark path of return (8.24–26).
body: The doctrine comes from *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.10 and *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* 6.2. The Gītā's point comes in {8.27}: the yogin who *knows* both paths is not deluded. Knowledge relativizes the cosmology.

glossary.short: Understanding: the discerning, deciding faculty, above the mind and the senses.
body: This translation always renders *buddhi* as "understanding." In Sāṅkhya psychology it is the first evolute of nature: the intellect that judges and wills. The Gītā's hierarchy runs senses, mind, understanding, then the self beyond understanding {3.42}, echoing *Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 3.10. The "understanding whose essence is resolve" is single, while that of the irresolute is "many-branched" {2.41}.

glossary.short: The yoga of understanding: acting from a settled, discerning mind rather than from desire.
body: In {2.49} it is contrasted with mere action. Action alone is inferior. What counts is the understanding from which one acts. God gives this yoga to devotees {10.10}.

glossary.short: "The final verse": 18.66, regarded by Śrīvaiṣṇavas as the culmination of the Gītā.
body: "Abandon all dharmas and take refuge in me alone." Śaṅkara reads it as renouncing all action for knowledge. Rāmānuja reads it as relying on God rather than on one's own means. Modern readers often take it as abandoning attachment to the results of dharma.

glossary.short: "The divine": fate, providence, unseen causes; the fifth factor of action (18.14).
body: The fifth of the five causes of every act, after the body, agent, instruments and efforts. It names the portion of any outcome beyond the agent's control.

glossary.short: The divine and demonic endowments: two moral natures (Chapter 16).
body: Chapter 16 sets out two clusters of character. The divine includes fearlessness, purity, generosity, non-harming and truth. The demonic includes hypocrisy, arrogance, anger and the creed that the world has no lord and is driven by desire alone. Its vivid portrait of the materialist {16.13–15} has been read as a critique of Lokāyata (Indian materialism).

glossary.short: Giving, generosity, the gift.
body: The sattvic gift is given "because it ought to be given," to one who cannot repay, at the right place and time {17.20}.

glossary.short: The embodied one: the self as dwelling in a body.
body: From *deha*, body. The term emphasizes that the self *has* a body as one wears clothes {2.22}. The guṇas "bind the imperishable embodied one in the body" {14.5}.

glossary.short: Right order: the law that holds the cosmos and society together, and the duty that falls to each being within it.
body: From the root *dhṛ*, "to hold, support." Dharma is what holds things in place: cosmic regularity, social law, ritual obligation, moral virtue, and the particular duty of a particular person. In the Mahābhārata it is famously "subtle" (*sūkṣma*). Its demands conflict, and the epic is largely a meditation on that conflict. The Gītā opens on "the field of dharma" {1.1}. Arjuna's crisis is a clash of dharmas: the warrior's duty to fight against the family dharmas he fears to destroy {1.40}. Kṛṣṇa answers on several levels. First comes one's own dharma {2.31}. Next, dharma performed without attachment {3.19}. Then dharma as what God descends to protect {4.7}. Finally comes the startling "abandon all dharmas and take refuge in me" {18.66}. How these levels fit together is one of the central interpretive questions of the text.

glossary.short: The blind Kuru king, father of the Kauravas; the Gītā's first speaker.
body: His blindness has been read symbolically: the attached father who cannot see dharma. His question, "what did my sons and the sons of Pāṇḍu do?", already divides the world into "mine" and "theirs."

glossary.short: Steadfastness, resolve: the power that holds a course.
body: Analyzed by the guṇas in {18.33–35}. Even steadfastness can be tamasic: the fool's stubborn grip on sleep, fear and grief.

glossary.short: Meditation: sustained, one-pointed contemplation.
body: Chapter 6 gives the Gītā's manual of meditation: posture, gaze, breath, diet, and the image of the lamp in a windless place {6.19}. In {12.12} meditation ranks above knowledge but below giving up the fruits of action, a striking reversal of the ascetic hierarchy.

glossary.short: Brāhmaṇa teacher of arms to both Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas; Arjuna's beloved guru.
Eldest son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, leader of the Kauravas.
Dualist Vedānta: God, souls and matter are eternally distinct.
body: Madhva's school reads the Gītā as teaching the eternal distinction between Viṣṇu and the souls who depend on him.

glossary.short: The pairs of opposites: heat and cold, pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor, success and failure.
body: To be "free of the pairs" {2.45} is to stop being yanked back and forth by every reversal of fortune. The same word names the copulative compound in Sanskrit grammar, and Kṛṣṇa says, "among compounds I am the *dvandva*" {10.33}.

glossary.short: M. K. Gandhi (1869–1948) called the Gītā his "spiritual dictionary" and translated it as Anāsaktiyoga, "the yoga of non-attachment."
body: Gandhi read the battle as allegory, the war within, and the Gītā as teaching selfless action consistent with non-violence. Critics have asked whether this does justice to a text in which God urges a warrior to fight.

glossary.short: Strand, quality: the three constituents of nature: sattva, rajas and tamas.
body: *Guṇa* means a strand of a rope. Nature is a cord twisted of three strands, and everything (food, faith, gifts, knowledge, happiness) is analyzed by their mixture (Chapters 14, 17, 18). To "go beyond the guṇas" (*guṇātīta*) is a mark of the liberated person {14.22–25}.

glossary.short: The senses: the five organs of perception (and five of action), the doors through which objects enter the mind.
body: Named after Indra ("belonging to Indra," powers). The senses are like a tortoise's limbs to be withdrawn {2.58}, and turbulent horses that carry off the mind {2.60, 2.67}. The chariot image of *Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 3.3–6 lies behind these verses.

glossary.short: Brief Upaniṣad that already joins renunciation with continued action.
body: "Doing works here, one may wish to live a hundred years; thus it is with you, not otherwise; action does not cling to a person" (*Īśā* 2). Many scholars see it as a seed of the Gītā's karma-yoga. Its verses on seeing all beings in the self {6.29} also anticipate the Gītā.

glossary.short: The Lord: God as sovereign ruler and inner controller of all beings.
body: "The Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, causing them to revolve by his māyā" {18.61}. The Gītā's God is both immanent (seated in the heart) and transcendent (greater than the imperishable).

glossary.short: King of Videha, model of the royal sage who reached perfection while ruling.
body: "Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone" {3.20}. Janaka is the questioner of Yājñavalkya in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* and the disciple in the *Aṣṭāvakra Gītā*.

glossary.short: The individual living being or soul; in 15.7, "a fragment of me."
body: God's "higher nature" is the *jīva-bhūta*, the life-principle that sustains the world {7.5}. The individual soul is "an eternal fragment (*aṁśa*) of me" {15.7}. Whether this fragment is ultimately identical with, distinct from, or a part of God is the fault line between the Vedānta schools.

glossary.short: Knowledge: liberating insight into the nature of the self and reality.
body: Not information but transformative recognition. "Nothing here purifies like knowledge" {4.38}; its fire burns all actions to ashes {4.37}. Śaṅkara makes knowledge alone the direct means of liberation. Rāmānuja makes it a component of devotion.

glossary.short: The discipline of knowledge: liberation through discriminating insight into the self.
body: In {3.3} Kṛṣṇa names two ancient paths: knowledge for the followers of Sāṅkhya, action for the yogins. Much of the Gītā's subtlety lies in showing that they converge {5.4–5}.

glossary.short: Marathi saint-poet (1275–1296) whose Jñāneśvarī is a celebrated vernacular commentary on the Gītā.
body: Composed when he was about sixteen, the *Jñāneśvarī* brought the Gītā into Marathi verse. It joins non-dual insight with devotion and became the foundation of the Vārkarī tradition.

glossary.short: Time, as destroyer: Kṛṣṇa's self-revelation in 11.32.
body: "I am time, the mighty destroyer of worlds" {11.32}. Time here is an active power that devours. Arjuna is told the warriors are already slain, and he is to be "merely the instrument."

glossary.short: Cosmic ages: a yuga is a world-age; a thousand yugas make a day of Brahmā; a kalpa is a cycle of creation.
body: Indian cosmology measures time in vast cycles. Beings emerge at Brahmā's dawn and dissolve at his dusk {8.18–19}. God sends them forth at the beginning of each kalpa {9.7}.

glossary.short: Desire, craving; also pleasure as one of the legitimate aims of life.
body: The Gītā names desire "the enemy here" {3.37}, an insatiable fire that covers knowledge. Yet Kṛṣṇa is also "desire not opposed to dharma" {7.11}. The problem is not desire as such but desire cut loose from right order. Kāma is one of the three gates of hell, with anger and greed {16.21}.

glossary.short: Action, any deed, ritual or ordinary, together with the binding consequences it sets in motion.
body: In the Vedic world *karma* first meant ritual action. By the Upaniṣads it had come to name the moral law by which actions bear fruit (*phala*) in this and later lives, binding the agent to saṁsāra. The Gītā's problem follows from this. If all action binds, liberation seems to require ceasing to act; yet "no one can remain even for a moment without acting" {3.5}. The Gītā's answer is that it is not action but attachment to its fruit that binds {2.47}.

glossary.short: The discipline of action: doing what must be done without attachment to its results.
body: Kṛṣṇa's first and most characteristic teaching. One acts fully but gives up claim on the fruit. Success and failure are met with equanimity (*samatva*), and the work is offered as sacrifice or to God. It answers the dilemma of action and liberation without requiring withdrawal from the world. Tilak (*Gītā Rahasya*, 1915) and Gandhi (*Anāsaktiyoga*, 1929) made it the key to the whole text and a charter for public engagement.

glossary.short: Kuntī's first-born son, raised by a charioteer; ally of Duryodhana and secretly Arjuna's elder brother.
body: Called "that son of a charioteer" {11.26}. The epic's great tragic figure, who learns his true birth and still keeps faith with his friend.

glossary.short: Pitiable weakness, poverty of spirit: Arjuna's self-diagnosis in 2.7.
body: Arjuna says his being is "struck by the flaw of *kārpaṇya*," a word covering both pity and meanness. It is the moment he turns from arguing to asking, and becomes a student.

glossary.short: Upaniṣad of the boy Naciketas and Death; the Gītā's closest Upaniṣadic source.
body: Several Gītā verses are near-quotations: the unborn, undying self {2.19–20} = *Kaṭha* 2.18–19; the marvel no one knows {2.29} ≈ *Kaṭha* 2.7; the hierarchy of senses, mind and understanding {3.42} ≈ *Kaṭha* 3.10; the inverted tree {15.1} ≈ *Kaṭha* 6.1. The *Kaṭha* also has the chariot image and the *śreyas/preyas* distinction.

glossary.short: The hundred sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, led by Duryodhana; the Pāṇḍavas' cousins and opponents.
body: Strictly both sides descend from Kuru. In usage "Kauravas" means Dhṛtarāṣṭra's party.

glossary.short: "Unmanliness": the faint-heartedness Kṛṣṇa first rebukes (2.3).
body: A harsh, gendered word of the warrior code. Kṛṣṇa's first response is a shaming appeal to honor. Only from {2.11} does he begin to teach. Vivekananda took {2.3} as the whole Gītā in one verse: "Yield not to weakness."

glossary.short: Anger: frustrated desire turned against its obstacle.
body: In {2.62} anger is born from thwarted desire. In {3.37} desire and anger are named together as one enemy, "born of rajas." The pairing anticipates modern psychology's treatment of anger as a response to blocked goals.

glossary.short: Prince of the Yādavas, Arjuna's charioteer and friend, revealed as the Blessed Lord; speaker of the Gītā.
body: "Kṛṣṇa" means "dark." In the epic he is a cousin and ally of the Pāṇḍavas, a statesman and strategist who will not bear arms. In the Gītā he speaks as God. Later traditions (*Harivaṁśa*, *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*) add the cowherd childhood in Vraja. Scholars debate how the epic hero, the Vāsudeva cult, and Viṣṇu came to be identified.

glossary.short: Member of the warrior-ruler order; Arjuna's class.
body: For a kṣatriya "nothing is better than a battle fought in accord with dharma" {2.31}. Heroism, vigor, generosity and leadership are his nature {18.43}.

glossary.short: The field: the body, and by extension all of nature as the arena of experience.
body: The Gītā opens on "the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus" {1.1}. Chapter 13 reveals the body itself as the field. The battlefield and the body are one image.

glossary.short: The knower of the field: the conscious self that witnesses the body and nature.
body: "Know that I am the knower of the field in all fields" {13.2}. Advaitins read this as the identity of self and God. Theists read it as God's indwelling in every knower.

glossary.short: Family dharma: the hereditary duties and rites that sustain a lineage.
body: The ground of Arjuna's first argument against fighting. His dharma is that of the clan. Kṛṣṇa will argue from a different level: the warrior's dharma, then the self, then God.

glossary.short: "The field of the Kurus": the plain north of Delhi where the war is fought; "the field of dharma."
"Standing on the summit," or "like an anvil": unchanging, immovable.
body: Commentators explain it as the anvil on which everything is hammered while it stays unchanged.

glossary.short: The holding-together of the world: action for the cohesion and welfare of society.
body: Even one who has nothing left to gain should act, to hold the world together and set an example {3.20–21}. God himself acts for this reason {3.22–24}. Tilak and Gandhi read it as the Gītā's social ethic.

glossary.short: Madhva (13th century), founder of Dvaita Vedānta; wrote two Gītā commentaries.
The great Sanskrit epic of the Bhārata war, of which the Gītā forms part (Bhīṣma Parvan 23–40).
body: Some 75,000 verses (in the Critical Edition) composed and expanded c. 400 BCE–400 CE. It tells of the feud between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas, culminating in an eighteen-day war at Kurukṣetra. The Gītā is narrated by Sañjaya to the blind king Dhṛtarāṣṭra just before the war begins. Its themes — dharma's subtlety, fate and effort, and the cost of violence — run through the whole epic.

glossary.short: Mind: the coordinating faculty that receives sense impressions and wanders after them.
body: Distinct from *buddhi*. The mind is restless "like the wind" {6.34} and must be steadied by practice and dispassion {6.35}. It is counted as the sixth sense {15.7}.

glossary.short: Māyā: God's power of appearance; the bewildering, creative power that both manifests and veils.
body: In the Gītā māyā is first of all divine power: Kṛṣṇa takes birth "by my own māyā" {4.6}. That same power veils him: "this divine māyā of mine, made of the guṇas, is hard to cross" {7.14}. Later Advaita develops māyā into the doctrine that the world is an appearance superimposed on brahman. The Gītā itself is less committal.

glossary.short: The school of Vedic ritual interpretation, focused on injunctions and their fruits.
body: The ritualists of {2.42–44}, who "delight in the letter of the Veda" for heavenly rewards, resemble the Mīmāṁsā outlook. The Gītā keeps its doctrine of duty but strips it of desire for fruit.

glossary.short: Liberation: release from the cycle of rebirth and the bondage of karma.
body: The final goal of Indian soteriology. The Gītā's distinctive claim is that liberation is compatible with full engagement in the world. Chapter 18 is titled "liberation through renunciation."

glossary.short: Freedom from action: the state of no longer being bound by karma, reached not by ceasing to act but by acting without attachment.
body: "Not by abstaining from actions does a person attain freedom from action" {3.4}. The Gītā turns the renunciant's ideal inside out. The goal of the monk (*naiṣkarmya*) is reached in the midst of action, by the one who "sees inaction in action" {4.18}.

glossary.short: "Merely the instrument": Arjuna's role in God's action (11.33).
body: One of the most morally fraught phrases in the text. Does it dissolve Arjuna's responsibility, or relocate it? It parallels the teaching that the self is not the doer {3.27}, {18.16}.

glossary.short: "Desireless action": action without craving for its fruit; the ethical core of karma-yoga.
body: The phrase is not in the Gītā itself, but it became the standard name for its teaching. It does not mean action without purpose. As Vivekananda insisted, the desireless worker is not "like a brute, nor inert, nor heartless." It means action whose purpose is the act's rightness, freed from the ego's stake in outcomes. Philosophers have compared it with Kant's duty for duty's sake, and have asked whether an agent can act well while indifferent to consequences.

glossary.short: The sacred syllable; with tat ("that") and sat ("being, good"), the threefold name of brahman (17.23).
body: Om is the "one-syllabled brahman" {8.13}, chanted at the beginning and end of Vedic recitation. In {17.23–27} *oṁ tat sat* sanctifies sacrifice, gift and austerity: Om to begin, *tat* to renounce the fruit, *sat* to affirm goodness.

glossary.short: The five sons of Pāṇḍu (Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Arjuna, Nakula, Sahadeva), the epic's heroes.
body: Divinely fathered, raised in exile, cheated of their kingdom at dice. Their claim to the throne is the war's cause.

glossary.short: The fruit of action: its result, reward, or karmic consequence.
body: The image is agricultural: deeds are seeds that ripen. Renouncing the fruit (*karma-phala-tyāga*) is, for the Gītā, the essence of true renunciation {18.2}. Note that the verse forbids making the fruit one's *motive* (*hetu*) {2.47}. It does not forbid foreseeing consequences.

glossary.short: Nature: the dynamic matrix of matter, mind and energy, made of the three guṇas.
body: In Sāṅkhya, prakṛti evolves into intellect, ego, mind, senses and elements. All activity is hers. The Gītā makes her God's own nature: lower (eightfold, material) and higher (the life-principle) {7.4–5}. "Actions are performed in every case by the guṇas of nature" {3.27}. This is the basis of the teaching that the self is not the doer.

glossary.short: Breath, vital energy; prāṇāyāma is its regulation.
body: The in-breath and out-breath (*prāṇa, apāna*) are offered into each other as a sacrifice {4.29}. At death the yogin draws the breath between the eyebrows or into the head {8.10, 8.12}.

glossary.short: Surrender, taking refuge in God; developed by Śrīvaiṣṇavas from 18.66.
body: Rāmānuja's tradition made *prapatti* a distinct means of salvation: total surrender to God's grace, especially in reading {18.66}.

glossary.short: Serenity and grace: the mind's clarity, and God's favor; one word for both.
body: In {2.64–65} prasāda is the serenity of a mind freed from attraction and aversion. In {18.56–62} it is God's grace by which one reaches the eternal abode. The single word suggests that inner clarity and divine favor are two faces of one gift.

glossary.short: Person, spirit: in Sāṅkhya the pure conscious witness distinct from nature; in the Gītā also God as Supreme Person.
body: In classical Sāṅkhya, puruṣa is pure consciousness, many in number, inactive, merely witnessing nature's play. The Gītā takes over the polarity {13.19–23} and then crowns it with a third term. Beyond the perishable and the imperishable stands the Supreme Person {15.16–18}.

glossary.short: The aims of human life: dharma (right order), artha (wealth, power), kāma (pleasure), and mokṣa (liberation).
body: The rajasic person "holds to dharma, pleasure and wealth" out of attachment {18.34}, that is, the first three aims pursued for their fruits.

glossary.short: The Supreme Person: God as beyond both the perishable world and the imperishable self.
body: The title of Chapter 15 and the summit of the Gītā's theology. It is pivotal for theistic Vedānta (Rāmānuja, Madhva, the Vaiṣṇava schools). Advaitins read it as the absolute described from the standpoint of the world.

glossary.short: Attraction and aversion: the twin reflexes of liking and disliking that bind the mind to objects.
body: "Attraction and aversion lie in wait in the objects of each sense" {3.34}. The sage moves among objects with senses "free from attraction and aversion" {2.64}. Yoga-sūtra 2.7–8 makes the same pair two of the five afflictions (*kleśa*).

glossary.short: The guṇa of passion, activity, restlessness and craving.
body: Literally "dust, haze," that which colors. Desire and anger are "born of rajas" {3.37}. Its fruit is pain {14.16}.

glossary.short: Rāmānuja (traditionally 1017–1137), theologian of Viśiṣṭādvaita; his Gītā commentary centers on devotion.
body: Rāmānuja reads the Gītā as culminating in loving devotion (*bhakti*) to Nārāyaṇa. Knowledge and action are its auxiliaries. Against Śaṅkara he insists that selves and world are real.

glossary.short: Concentration, absorption: the settled, unified state of a mind fully gathered.
body: In the Gītā *samādhi* means steadiness of understanding more than trance {2.53}. Arjuna's question about the person "established in samādhi" {2.54} opens the portrait of the sage.

glossary.short: Equanimity, evenness: the mind's sameness in success and failure. "Equanimity is called yoga" (2.48).
body: The Gītā's most compact definition of yoga {2.48}. Equanimity is psychological (unshaken in gain and loss), ethical (seeing the same in the scholar and the outcaste {5.18}), and metaphysical (seeing the same brahman everywhere {5.19}). The three levels support one another.

glossary.short: Renunciation: giving up actions themselves; formally, the life of the wandering ascetic.
body: The Gītā redefines it. The true renunciant is one who does what should be done without depending on its fruit, not one who merely abandons the sacred fires {6.1}. In {18.2} Kṛṣṇa distinguishes saṁnyāsa (renouncing desire-driven acts) from tyāga (relinquishing the fruit of all acts).

glossary.short: The round of birth, death and rebirth, driven by karma and ignorance.
body: Literally "flowing together, wandering." The Gītā images it as an ocean of death {12.7}, as the coming and going of those who seek heaven {9.21}, and as the upside-down world-tree {15.1–3}.

glossary.short: Attachment, clinging: the bond between the self and an object or outcome.
body: Literally "sticking-together." In the causal chain of {2.62–63}, dwelling on objects produces attachment, attachment produces desire, and desire produces anger and ruin. Non-attachment (*asaṅga*) is the axe that cuts down the world-tree {15.3}.

glossary.short: Dhṛtarāṣṭra's charioteer and bard, granted divine sight by Vyāsa to narrate the battle.
body: The Gītā is thus doubly framed. We hear Kṛṣṇa through Sañjaya, telling a blind king, inside an epic recited by Vyāsa's disciple.

glossary.short: Ādi Śaṅkara (c. 8th century CE), founder-systematizer of Advaita Vedānta; author of the oldest surviving Gītā commentary.
body: His *Gītā-bhāṣya* argues that liberation comes through knowledge alone. Action cannot coexist with knowledge of the actionless self. Karma-yoga therefore prepares the mind but is transcended by renunciation. He reads {18.66} as renouncing all action.

glossary.short: "Enumeration": the dualist philosophy of puruṣa and prakṛti; in the Gītā also simply "discriminating understanding."
body: In the Gītā "Sāṅkhya" does not yet mean the later classical system of Īśvarakṛṣṇa (c. 350–450 CE). It means an older, theistic proto-Sāṅkhya and, more broadly, the way of discriminative knowledge {2.39}, {3.3}. Its categories (guṇas, the evolutes of nature, the inactive witness) structure Chapters 13, 14 and 18.

glossary.short: Authoritative teaching, scripture: the injunctions that determine what should and should not be done.
body: "Let scripture be your standard" {16.24}. Chapter 16 ends on scriptural authority, yet Chapter 17 immediately asks about those who act with faith outside scripture.

glossary.short: Being and non-being; real and unreal; good and not-good.
body: "Of the unreal there is no coming to be; of the real there is no ceasing to be" {2.16}. This is the Gītā's most compressed metaphysical axiom. God is both *sat* and *asat* {9.19} and what is beyond both {11.37}. Brahman is "neither being nor non-being" {13.12}.

glossary.short: The guṇa of clarity, goodness, light and balance.
body: From *sat*, "being, good." Sattva illuminates and harmonizes, but it still binds, "by attachment to happiness and to knowledge" {14.6}. The word also means "being, essence" ({10.36}, {17.3}).

glossary.short: Faith: trust, orientation of the heart toward what one holds true and good.
body: "A person is made of faith: whatever one's faith is, that is what one is" {17.3}. Faith is not belief in propositions but the shape of one's deepest commitment, and it too comes in three guṇa-kinds.

glossary.short: The better, the highest good: what is truly beneficial, as against the merely pleasant (preyas).
body: Arjuna asks to be told "decisively what is better" {2.7}. The distinction of *śreyas* and *preyas* comes from *Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 2.1–2.

glossary.short: "What is heard" (revealed Veda) and "what is remembered" (tradition); also simply hearing and memory.
body: Formally the Gītā is *smṛti*, part of the epic, but tradition treats it as having the authority of an Upaniṣad. Arjuna's final words play on the other sense: "I have regained my memory (*smṛti*)" {18.73}.

glossary.short: The person "steady in wisdom": the Gītā's portrait of the sage (2.54–72).
body: Arjuna asks how such a person speaks, sits and moves {2.54}. The answer is a portrait. The sage is content in the self, unshaken in sorrow, withdraws the senses like a tortoise, and stays full like the ocean while rivers flow in. Gandhi had these verses recited daily at his prayer meetings.

glossary.short: Member of the serving order, the fourth varṇa.
body: {9.32} declares that śūdras, with women and vaiśyas, reach the supreme goal by taking refuge in God. It was a radical opening of liberation beyond the Vedic elite, though framed in hierarchical language.

glossary.short: Own-being, inherent nature: the innate disposition from which one's actions flow.
body: "Your nature will compel you" {18.59–60}. Svabhāva grounds both the determinism of nature and the dignity of each person's own path.

glossary.short: One's own dharma: the duty proper to one's nature, station and stage of life.
body: "Better one's own dharma, though imperfect, than another's dharma well performed" {3.35}, {18.47}. The doctrine ties duty to one's nature (*svabhāva*) and was historically read in terms of caste. Modern readers (Gandhi, Aurobindo, many contemporary teachers) reinterpret it as vocation: the work that fits one's actual temperament and capacities. Either way, its philosophical point is that the good is not one-size-fits-all. Imitating another's path, however admirable, is "dangerous."

glossary.short: The guṇa of darkness, inertia, dullness and delusion.
body: Tamas binds by negligence, laziness and sleep {14.8}. Vivekananda saw Arjuna's refusal to fight as tamas disguised as sattva: fear masquerading as compassion.

glossary.short: Austerity: "heat," disciplined effort and self-restraint; one of the three sanctifying acts.
body: From *tap*, "to heat." Chapter 17 distinguishes austerity of body, speech and mind, and condemns self-torture as demonic {17.5–6}.

glossary.short: B. G. Tilak (1856–1920), nationalist leader; his Gītā Rahasya reads the Gītā as a gospel of action.
body: Written in Mandalay jail (published 1915), the *Gītā Rahasya* argues against Śaṅkara that the Gītā's final teaching is energetic, selfless action for the world's welfare. It was intellectual armor for the independence movement.

glossary.short: Relinquishment: giving up the fruit of actions, not the actions themselves.
body: "One who relinquishes the fruit of action is called a relinquisher" {18.11}. Chapter 18 classifies relinquishment by the guṇas. Giving up duty out of delusion is tamasic. Giving it up for fear of hardship is rajasic. Doing duty because it ought to be done, without attachment, is sattvic {18.7–9}.

glossary.short: The philosophical texts concluding the Veda (c. 800–200 BCE), source of the doctrines of ātman and brahman.
body: The Gītā calls itself an Upaniṣad in its colophons and quotes or echoes them repeatedly: *Kaṭha* above all, also *Īśā*, *Śvetāśvatara*, *Muṇḍaka*, *Chāndogya*. A traditional verse calls the Upaniṣads the cows, Kṛṣṇa the milker, Arjuna the calf, and the Gītā the milk.

glossary.short: Dispassion: the fading of craving for objects.
body: Literally "loss of color," the fading of the passion (*rāga*) that colors the mind.

glossary.short: Member of the order of farmers, herders and traders.
The four social orders of brahmanical theory: brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya and śūdra.
body: Literally "color, class." Kṛṣṇa says he created the four orders "according to the division of guṇa and action" {4.13}. Whether the Gītā means birth-based caste or qualities of character is contested. Traditional commentators largely assume birth. Reformers (Vivekananda, Gandhi in part, Aurobindo, Ambedkar's critics and critics of Ambedkar) argue over whether quality-based readings are faithful or apologetic. B. R. Ambedkar read the Gītā as a defense of caste. That reading must be taken seriously.

glossary.short: "Mixing of the orders": the confusion of social classes Arjuna fears as the fruit of war.
body: Arjuna's chain of fears {1.40–44} runs: war kills the men, family dharma collapses, women are "corrupted," orders mix, ancestors fall. The argument reveals how deeply his ethics is tied to lineage. Kṛṣṇa turns the word back on Arjuna: if God ceased to act, *he* would cause confusion {3.24}.

glossary.short: The Veda: the oldest scriptures (Ṛg, Sāma, Yajur, later Atharva), with their ritual and philosophical appendices.
body: The Gītā is ambivalent. It criticizes those who "delight in the letter of the Veda" for heavenly rewards {2.42–44} and calls the Vedas useless to the knower as a well in a flood {2.46}. Yet God is "what is to be known through all the Vedas" {15.15}, and the world-tree's leaves are Vedic hymns {15.1}.

glossary.short: "End of the Veda": the Upaniṣads and the philosophical schools that interpret them through three foundational texts.
body: Classical Vedānta rests on the *prasthāna-traya*, the "triple foundation": the Upaniṣads, the *Brahma-sūtra*, and the Bhagavad Gītā. Every major Vedāntin therefore wrote a Gītā commentary.

glossary.short: Extended power, manifestation: the excellences through which God is visible in the world.
body: Chapter 10 lists them: among lights the sun, among mountains Meru, among letters A. "Whatever being has power, splendor, or vigor arises from a fraction of my brilliance" {10.41}. Theologically, God is to be found in the excellent and the extraordinary.

glossary.short: Discernment: knowledge made specific, realized, or applied; paired with jñāna.
body: The pair *jñāna-vijñāna* recurs. Commentators differ: general vs. specific knowledge, theoretical vs. experiential knowledge, knowledge of the unmanifest vs. of the manifest God. Chapter 7 is titled by the pair.

glossary.short: Despair, dejection: Arjuna's state in Chapter 1, "the yoga of Arjuna's despair."
body: That a chapter of pure despair is called a *yoga* has prompted reflection. Crisis is the first step of the path.

glossary.short: Qualified non-dualism: God is the one reality, with souls and world as his real body or modes.
body: Rāmānuja's school. The Gītā is read as teaching devotion to a personal God, Nārāyaṇa, whose body is the universe. Selves are real and eternal, distinct yet inseparable from him.

glossary.short: The universal form: the cosmic vision of God shown to Arjuna in Chapter 11.
body: Given a divine eye, Arjuna sees all worlds in Kṛṣṇa's body. He sees "the light of a thousand suns" {11.12}, and then the warriors of both armies rushing into God's mouths. It is one of the great theophanies of world literature. J. Robert Oppenheimer recalled {11.12} and {11.32} at the first atomic test.

glossary.short: Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902), disciple of Ramakrishna, who presented Vedānta and the Gītā to the West.
body: Vivekananda saw the Gītā's originality in two things: harmonizing the paths of yoga, knowledge and devotion, and "work without desire." He took {2.3} as its whole message: strength, not weakness. His lectures *Karma Yoga* (1896) made the Gītā's ethic famous in the West.

glossary.short: The legendary author of the Mahābhārata and arranger of the Vedas.
body: Also grandfather of both Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas, a character inside his own epic. Vivekananda notes "Vyāsa" was a title borne by many.

glossary.short: Sacrifice: the Vedic ritual offering, and by extension any action offered beyond the self.
body: In the Vedic world sacrifice sustains the cosmos. Gods and humans nourish one another {3.11}, and food, rain and sacrifice form a wheel {3.14–16}. The Gītā interiorizes and universalizes it. Breath-control, study, self-restraint and knowledge are all sacrifices {4.25–33}, and "brahman is the offering" {4.24}. Action done "for the sake of sacrifice" does not bind {3.9}.

glossary.short: Literally "yoking": discipline, method, concentration, union; in the Gītā, any integrated path that binds the self to the highest.
body: The word yokes many meanings: harnessing horses, applying a method, concentrating the mind, joining with God. The Gītā defines it as equanimity {2.48}, as "skill in actions" {2.50}, and as "unyoking from union with sorrow" {6.23}. Every chapter is titled a "yoga." God's own creative power is also "my sovereign yoga" {9.5}, and Kṛṣṇa is "lord of yoga" {18.78}.

glossary.short: The classical school of Yoga, codified in Patañjali's Yoga-sūtra (c. 2nd–5th c. CE).
body: The *Yoga-sūtra* is probably later than the Gītā but shares its vocabulary: practice and dispassion (YS 1.12, Gītā {6.35}), the afflictions of attraction and aversion, and concentration.

glossary.short: "Gaining and keeping": acquisition and security. God secures it for exclusive devotees (9.22).
body: In {2.45} Arjuna is told to be free of "acquiring and keeping." In {9.22} God promises to provide it. Today it is the motto of the Life Insurance Corporation of India.

glossary.short: Yoked: disciplined, integrated, concentrated, joined to the highest.
body: The past participle of the root of *yoga*. The translation keeps "yoked" throughout so that the reader can hear the single image: the person whose faculties are harnessed together and steered. The unyoked (*ayukta*) are dragged by their senses {2.66}.
